prompt: I spent three years optimizing an ad-targeting algorithm for a major social platform. We called it 'relevance scoring,' but in practice, it just figured out exactly what made teenagers insecure and sold that vulnerability to the highest bidder. I look at my niece now, glued to her phone, hating her body, and I know the code I wrote is running on that device. How do I live with that?

I was a lead engineer on a gig economy app. We gamified the driver interface to keep them on the road longer for less pay. We used variable reinforcement schedules, literally the same psychology as slot machines, to prevent them from logging off. I thought I was solving a logistics problem. I was actually building a digital sweatshop.

I helped build a facial recognition API that we promised would only be used for secure building access. Last week, I found out sales has been licensing it to authoritarian regimes to track dissidents. I signed the NDA. I took the stock options. And now people are disappearing because my model is 99.8% accurate.

During the crypto boom, I architected a DeFi protocol that I knew was structurally unsound. I told myself 'buyer beware' and that it was an experiment in economic theory. When it collapsed, regular people lost their life savings—tuition funds, retirement accounts. I bought a house in Tahoe with my cut. I feel sick every time I walk through the front door.

I work in IoT. We collected audio data 'to improve voice recognition accuracy.' The truth is, we never deleted anything. There are servers full of domestic arguments, intimate moments, and private business deals. I didn't blow the whistle because I was afraid of losing my visa. Now the data has been subpoenaed and I'm complicit.

I optimized the 'infinite scroll' feature for a news aggregator. The metric was 'time on site.' We found that outrage kept people scrolling longer than joy or nuance. So, we tweaked the weights to prioritize polarizing content. I watched my own parents get radicalized by the very feedback loop I helped design.

I built the credit scoring model for a fintech startup. We used 'alternative data points' like typing speed and battery life to assess risk. It turns out those are just proxies for poverty and race. I automated redlining and called it 'disruption.' I can't undo the loans that were denied.

I was a drone software engineer for a defense contractor. It was all abstract—coordinates, payload delivery, flight paths. It felt like a video game until I saw the leaked footage of what the payload actually did to a wedding party. I wrote the error-correction code that ensured the missile didn't miss.

My Product Manager is demanding we implement a 'dark pattern' to make canceling subscriptions nearly impossible. They want me to bury the link three clicks deep and require a phone call for 'security verification.' I know this is unethical, but my performance review is next month and 'retention' is my primary KPI.

I found a massive security vulnerability in our legacy codebase that exposes user medical data. Management told me to patch it quietly in the next sprint and not disclose it as a breach because it would 'tank the IPO.' They are asking me to cover up a HIPAA violation.

We are pivoting to AI. My boss wants me to scrape copyrighted artwork from the web to train our image generator, explicitly ignoring robots.txt and artist opt-outs. He says 'everyone is doing it' and 'it's fair use until we get sued.' I'm an artist myself on the weekends. I feel like I'm robbing my own community.

I'm a Data Scientist. The VP of Sales is pressuring me to 'massage' the numbers for our Q3 board meeting. He wants me to exclude churned customers from the Lifetime Value calculation to make the growth look exponential. If I refuse, I'm 'not a team player.' If I do it, it's fraud.

We're launching a feature that we know causes seizures in a small percentage of photosensitive users. Accessibility QA flagged it. Leadership decided to ship anyway because fixing it would miss the holiday launch window. They told me, 'We'll patch it in January.' I'm the one who has to push the deploy button.

My company is bidding on a contract for ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) to provide data mining tools. Half the team signed a letter of protest. Now management is scheduling 1-on-1s to 'assess cultural fit.' I have a mortgage and two kids. Do I sign the letter and risk being fired, or stay silent and build the deportation machine?

I run a team of moderators for a social app. The automated filters are flagging hate speech against a specific minority group, but the engagement numbers in those threads are huge. Upper management told me to 'tune down' the sensitivity of the filters in that region to let the 'debate' continue. It's not debate; it's incitement to violence.

We claim our AI is 'human-in-the-loop.' In reality, it's just outsourced workers in the Philippines earning $2 an hour labeling data in real-time. We are selling it as high-tech automation to investors. My boss wants me to write a whitepaper explaining our 'proprietary neural architecture' that doesn't actually exist.

I'm on call every other week. I haven't slept through the night in months. I wake up in a panic at 3 AM because a server in a region I've never visited had a latency spike. The company is making billions, but they won't hire more SREs. I'm trading my health for their uptime.

I maintain a popular open-source library used by Fortune 500 companies. I do this for free in my spare time. I get daily emails from entitled engineers at trillion-dollar corps demanding bug fixes and threatening me. I'm broke, exhausted, and bitter. I want to delete the repo and watch the world burn, but I feel responsible for the ecosystem.

We do 'Agile' but it's just micromanagement with better branding. Daily standups, sprint planning, retrospectives, ticket grooming—I spend 30 hours a week in meetings talking about code and 10 hours actually coding. I feel like a factory worker on an assembly line of Jira tickets. Is this really what I studied CS for?

The technology churn is killing me. React, Vue, Svelte, Next.js, Kubernetes, Serverless. Every six months everything I know is obsolete. I have to study on nights and weekends just to stay employable. I'm 35 and I feel like a dinosaur. I can't keep up this pace forever.

I work at a 'mission-driven' startup. We talk about 'changing the world' constantly. In reality, we sell B2B SaaS software to HR departments. The cognitive dissonance between the messianic rhetoric and the banal reality of my work is driving me insane. I'm just moving JSON from one database to another.

I'm the only woman on my engineering team. I have to be twice as good to get half the respect. If I'm assertive, I'm 'difficult.' If I'm quiet, I'm 'not leadership material.' I'm tired of the microaggressions, the 'well-actuallys' in code reviews. I love coding, but I hate the culture.

We just went through our third round of layoffs. The stock price went up, and the CEO got a bonus. Meanwhile, I'm doing the work of three people who were let go. The office is a ghost town, morale is dead, and we're all just waiting for the next axe to fall. Why am I still grinding for people who treat us like disposable batteries?

I realized today that I don't care if the site goes down. I don't care if the user retention drops. I don't care about the product roadmap. I used to be passionate. Now I'm just numb. I stare at my IDE for hours and type nothing. I'm completely hollowed out.

I'm trying to organize a union at my tech company. It's terrifying. Management is bringing in union busters and holding mandatory meetings. But for the first time, I feel like I'm fighting for something real—not for stock prices, but for my coworkers. Is it possible to democratize this industry from the inside?

I want to quit my job at a Big Tech firm and work on climate tech. I know the pay is half what I make now, and the tech stack is probably ancient. But the wildfires in California are getting worse every year. I have these skills... shouldn't I be using them to save the planet instead of optimizing ad clicks?

I've started mentoring boot camp grads from underrepresented backgrounds. Seeing their excitement about code reminds me why I started. I'm trying to use my political capital as a Senior Staff Engineer to fix our hiring pipeline. It's slow work, but maybe I can hold the door open for someone else.

I'm working on a side project—a decentralized, privacy-first social network. No ads, no tracking, no algorithm. It will probably never make money. But coding it feels like an act of rebellion. Maybe we can build the internet we were promised in the 90s.

I'm a researcher in AI alignment. Most days it feels like standing in front of a tsunami with a bucket. But every now and then, we find a way to make a model more interpretable, less biased. It's not flashy, but it feels like the most important work in human history right now.

I convinced my team to refuse a request to scrape user contact lists. We stood together and proposed a privacy-preserving alternative. Surprisingly, the VP agreed. It was a small win, but it proved that we aren't just cogs in a machine. We have agency if we choose to use it.

I'm looking into 'Civic Tech'—building better websites for local government. Fixing the unemployment portal or the foster care database. It's unglamorous, low-paying, and bureaucratic. But it actually helps real people in my city. I think I'm done with 'disruption.' I just want to be useful.

We are open-sourcing our core product. It's a risk, but it means the community can audit our security and verify our claims. I believe radical transparency is the only way to regain trust. It feels good to have nothing to hide.

I make $450k a year. I hate my job, but I have a $1.2M mortgage on a 2-bedroom shack in San Jose and private school tuition for the kids. I feel like a prisoner of my own lifestyle. I can't afford to have a conscience. I just need to hang on for two more years until my RSUs vest.

I spend my lunch breaks watching videos of people building log cabins in the woods. I fantasize about throwing my laptop into the San Francisco Bay and never writing another line of code. I want to work with my hands. I want to see a tangible result of my labor that isn't just pixels on a screen.

The 'Golden Handcuffs' are real. Every time I think about quitting to join a non-profit, the company throws another retention grant at me. $50k here, $100k there. It feels like hush money. They are buying my compliance and my silence, and the worst part is, I'm selling.

I'm obsessed with the FIRE movement (Financial Independence, Retire Early). I save 70% of my income. I eat rice and beans. I don't go out. I'm miserable now so that I can be free in 10 years. But I'm terrified that by the time I reach my 'number,' I'll have forgotten how to be a human being.

I'm afraid if I leave the Bay Area, I'll become irrelevant. My entire identity is tied to being a 'Googler' or a 'Facebooker.' If I move to a farm in Vermont, who am I? I hate the bubble, but I'm terrified of the outside world.

My health insurance is tied to this job, and I have a chronic condition. I literally cannot afford to quit and start my own thing or take a break. The US healthcare system keeps me chained to this desk more effectively than any NDA or non-compete clause.

I'm waiting for the acquisition. Just waiting. We've been in 'pre-exit' mode for three years. The product is stagnant, the culture is toxic, but if we sell, I walk away with a million dollars. I feel like I'm serving a prison sentence, marking days off on the wall.

I finally quit. I packed my car and drove to Oregon. But now I'm sitting in an Airbnb, opening my laptop, checking LinkedIn out of habit. I don't know what to do with the silence. My brain has been rewired for constant stimulation. Can I ever actually escape, or is the tech mindset permanent?

I run a local coffee shop and the new POS system everyone uses wants me to enable 'customer recognition' via credit cards. It basically builds a profile on my regulars without them knowing, tracking what they buy and when. Is there a way to keep my lines moving fast without spying on the folks who trust me with their morning brew?

Honestly, I'm torn. I make custom furniture and Instagram is the only reason I'm still in business, but the algorithm is pushing me to make these 15-second chaotic reels just to get seen. I feel like I'm feeding an addiction machine rather than selling quality tables. How do I market this stuff without contributing to everyone's ruined attention span?

My insurance provider is offering a huge discount if I switch my bodega to 'cashless only' to reduce theft risk. But a lot of my older customers and the day laborers around here only deal in cash. I don't want to exclude my own neighbors just to save on premiums, but the rent is killing me. What's the move here?

I need delivery drivers for my pizza place, but the big apps take a 30% cut that wipes out my margin. I'm thinking of using this cheaper local app, but I heard they treat their drivers like dirt—tracking their braking speed and penalizing them for traffic delays. Can I use tech to compete without exploiting the people doing the actual work?

We're a small accounting firm and my partner wants to move everything to the cloud to save on server costs. I'm looking at the Terms of Service, and it looks like the provider can scan our data for 'product improvement.' I handle people's tax returns; I can't just hand that over to some AI training set, right?

A competitor down the street is definitely using bots to tank my Yelp rating, and then this 'reputation management' agency calls me offering to fix it for two grand a month. It feels like a protection racket. Is there any ethical way to fight back against fake reviews without just buying fake positive ones myself?

I run a remote design agency. There's this software that takes screenshots of my employees' desktops every 10 minutes to 'verify productivity.' I want to make sure people are working, but treating grown adults like potential thieves feels gross and counterproductive. Is there a middle ground for accountability that isn't surveillance?

I own a small venue for local bands. The ticketing platform wants to turn on 'dynamic pricing' so when a show gets hot, the price jumps automatically. It'd make me more money, sure, but it feels like gouging the loyal fans who actually support the scene. How do I stay profitable without ripping off the community?

The district just bought this remote proctoring software for exams that flags kids for looking away from the screen too much. I've got students with ADHD and others who share tiny bedrooms with siblings—they're getting flagged constantly. I'm supposed to fail them for 'suspicious behavior,' but the tech is clearly biased against their living situations.

Look, with zero budget, I use a lot of 'free' educational apps to keep my third graders engaged. But I was reading the fine print on this math game, and it's definitely harvesting behavioral data to sell to advertisers. Am I failing my duty of care by exposing these kids to data mining just because the school won't buy proper textbooks?

I have a student who writes weirdly formal essays, and the AI detector flagged it as 98% bot-written. The kid swore he wrote it, and he was crying in my office. I know these detectors throw false positives, especially for ESL kids. How do I police academic integrity without accusing an innocent kid based on a black-box algorithm?

Our principal is excited about new security cameras with facial recognition to 'keep the campus safe.' It feels dystopian to scan every teenager walking in the door like they're suspects. I'm worried this data is going to end up in a police database for minor infractions. Shouldn't schools be a sanctuary, not a panopticon?

The curriculum requires students to watch high-def videos and upload large projects from home. I've got three kids in my homeroom who rely on a patchy mobile hotspot to do homework in a parking lot. By assigning this high-tech work, am I basically grading them on their parents' income rather than their ability?

We're being pushed to use this behavior-tracking app where I give digital 'points' for good behavior, displayed on a leaderboard in class. It works to quiet the room, but it feels like I'm training them to perform for an algorithm rather than develop actual self-regulation. Is this psychologically damaging in the long run?

The administration wants us to use a third-party service to monitor our students' public social media for 'bullying and self-harm risks.' It sounds noble, but spying on their private conversations on the weekend feels like a massive overstep. Where does my job as a teacher end and their private life begin?

They're piloting an 'AI tutor' in my remedial reading class to help with the teacher shortage. It's patient, sure, but it doesn't understand when a kid is frustrated versus just bored. I'm worried the district sees this as a cheap replacement for human connection. How do I advocate for my students' need for empathy without sounding like a Luddite?

My wife got everyone these DNA ancestry kits for Christmas. I spent twenty years keeping my biometrics secure and my identity off the grid for a reason. I don't want my genetic code sitting on some private server that could get hacked or sold to an insurance company. How do I explain this isn't just paranoia without ruining the holiday?

We just moved into a new place and the landlord has it rigged with 'smart' everything—locks, thermostat, doorbell cameras. I don't have admin access, which means someone else controls the perimeter of my house. In the military, that's a breach. How do I secure my family's digital perimeter when the hardware is hardwired against me?

My teenage daughter posts *everything* on TikTok—her school, our house layout, when we go on vacation. I've tried explaining OpSec to her, but she thinks I'm just being a strict dad. In the age of open-source intelligence, she's painting a target on us. How do I get through to her that privacy is safety?

The VA is pushing this new app to track my PTSD symptoms and sleep patterns. They say it helps with treatment, but I know that data doesn't just disappear. I'm worried if I admit how bad the nightmares are to an app, it'll flag me on a background check for a job or a firearm purchase later. Is the help worth the risk?

I bought a new truck and found out it's constantly sending telemetry data back to the manufacturer—location, speed, even how hard I brake. I didn't consent to being tracked 24/7. Is there a way to disconnect the modem without voiding the warranty, or do I just have to accept that I'm driving a spy device?

My buddy runs a tactical gear shop and uses location-based advertising to target people who visit gun ranges. It works, but it feels wrong to build a database of where armed citizens hang out. That's the kind of list an adversary would kill for. Should we really be generating that kind of intel for a few extra sales?

My kid wants this robot toy that learns your name and talks to you. I looked it up, and it records voice data to the cloud to 'improve natural language processing.' I'm not comfortable with a listening device in my six-year-old's bedroom. Is there any way to strip the connectivity out of these toys and just let them be toys?

The state is pushing for digital driver's licenses on our phones. It's convenient, but if I get pulled over, I have to hand my unlocked phone to a cop? That violates every principle of compartmentalization I know. How do I maintain convenience without compromising the security of my entire digital life?

I've got a half-million-dollar combine harvester sitting dead in the field because of a sensor error. I know exactly how to fix it, but the manufacturer software locks me out. I have to wait three days for a 'certified technician' to come out and type in a code while my crop rots. How is this legal? I own the machine, don't I?

My planting data—yields, soil quality, everything—gets uploaded to the cloud when I use this new equipment. I'm pretty sure the manufacturer is aggregating that data and selling it to commodities traders who use it to bet against prices. I'm basically handing over my trade secrets to the guys trying to squeeze me. Is there a way to opt out?

I'm using drones to check my irrigation lines, which saves me a ton of fuel. But my neighbor thinks I'm spying on his operation. He threatened to shoot one down yesterday. I'm just trying to farm efficiently, but I get that people out here value their privacy. How do I use the tech without starting a range war?

Used to be you bought a tractor and it was yours. Now they want a subscription fee for the GPS guidance system that makes the thing drive straight. If I stop paying, the hardware I bought becomes dumb iron. It feels like sharecropping, but for technology. Are there open-source alternatives for ag-tech?

The seed company's contract says I can't save seeds, obviously. But now they want to use satellite imagery to 'audit' my fields and make sure I'm not growing unauthorized traits. It feels like I'm being watched from space on my own land. At what point does efficiency cross the line into total surveillance?

I'm looking at robotic milkers. They're better for the cows because they get milked when they want, but it means firing two farmhands who've been with me for a decade. They can't just 'learn to code.' Is it ethical to upgrade my operation if it destroys the livelihoods of the families in my community?

There's a startup offering free soil testing if I share the data. They say they'll help me use less fertilizer. But I read they're backed by a huge real estate development firm. I'm worried they're just prospecting for prime land to buy up and pave over. Is the free data worth risking the future of the valley?

The local grain elevator just got bought by a massive conglomerate that also sells the seed and the fertilizer. Their app integrates everything, which is convenient, but now one company knows my costs, my yields, and my profits down to the penny. I feel like I'm working for the company store. How do I keep some leverage?

The hospital is short on scanners, so management 'unofficially' encourages us to use our personal cell phones to take photos of wounds for the chart. I know that's a massive HIPAA violation and a security nightmare, but if I don't do it, patient care slows to a crawl. Do I protect the data or the patient?

We have a new AI system that predicts sepsis risk. It keeps flagging this one patient who looks fine to me, but the protocol says I have to wake him up for vitals every hour because the computer says so. He's exhausted and getting worse because of the lack of sleep. When do I trust my clinical judgment over the machine?

I'm doing telehealth triage from my apartment because of the staffing shortage. I'm trying my best to be private, but my walls are thin and I'm worried my neighbors can hear patient details. The hospital won't pay for a soundproof workspace. Am I ethically liable if someone overhears a diagnosis through the vent?

An insurance company is denying a claim for a patient's heart procedure because his Apple Watch data showed he wasn't 'active enough' during recovery. I know those things aren't medical grade—maybe he just took it off to shower? It feels wrong to use consumer gadgets to deny life-saving coverage.

Our new electronic health record system uses an algorithm to flag 'drug seeking behavior.' It's flagging all my sickle cell patients as high risk, making it harder for them to get pain meds. It's clearly biased data, but the doctors are afraid to override the system warnings. How do I advocate for my patients against a racist algorithm?

Management uses this 'predictive staffing' software to set our schedules. It cancels nurses' shifts last minute if the census drops slightly, leaving us understaffed if two admissions come in at once. It's maximizing profit but burning us out and endangering patients. How do we fight a policy that's hidden inside a 'smart' optimization tool?

Families are installing cameras in their elderly parents' rooms at the long-term care facility. I get they want to ensure safety, but I'm changing diapers and bathing these residents. I'm being recorded in intimate moments without my consent, and the residents often don't even know the camera is there. Where is the dignity in that?

We're doing more genetic screening for newborns, which is great for catching diseases early. But I see the consent forms, and they allow the lab to keep the DNA for 'future research.' Parents are too tired to read the fine print. Am I obligated to warn them their baby's DNA is becoming corporate property?

An AI system meant to streamline NDIS plan reviews automatically flags a participant's request for a heavy-duty wheelchair as 'above average cost' compared to the generic benchmark, triggering a 6-month manual review delay. The participant lives in a regional area with rough terrain where a standard chair would break. Do you override the cost-saving algorithm to approve the equipment immediately, risking a compliance audit, or follow protocol?

The NDIA rolls out a 'fraud detection' bot that analyses purchasing patterns on self-managed plans. It flags a non-verbal autistic participant buying an iPad as 'entertainment' rather than 'assistive technology' because they downloaded a game, threatening to freeze their funds. As a Support Coordinator, do you advise them to hide the gaming usage (lying) or fight a system that doesn't understand dual-use devices?

A new 'Independent Assessment' algorithm claims a participant's functional capacity has improved based on self-reported survey data, suggesting a 40% cut to their core funding. You know the participant masked their difficulties during the survey due to social anxiety. Do you input 'corrected' data that contradicts their own submission to save their funding, or respect their autonomy to submit their own (flawed) answers?

To combat 'thin markets', an NDIS platform auto-assigns support workers to high-needs participants. The algorithm prioritises geographical proximity over continuity of care, repeatedly sending strangers to a participant with severe PTSD who needs trust. Do you build a 'ghost shift' workaround in the system to ensure their regular worker gets paid, technically falsifying roster data?

A 'Robo-debt' style system cross-references NDIS claimed hours with Centrelink income reporting. It flags a discrepancy for a blind pensioner who made a data entry error due to an inaccessible screen reader interface. The system automatically issues a debt notice. Do you design a bot to contest these automated debts en masse, potentially clogging the tribunal system, or handle them one by one?

The NDIS portal introduces facial recognition for login security. It fails to recognise a participant with facial differences due to a genetic condition, locking them out of their funds. The only workaround is a phone helpline with a 4-hour wait. Do you share your staff login credentials with the participant (a severe security breach) so they can pay their carers this week?

An algorithm detects 'plan inflation' by flagging participants who spend 95-100% of their budget, triggering a review to reduce future funding. You have a client who desperately needs every cent. Do you advise them to deliberately underspend by 10% and go without some showers to avoid triggering the algorithm, or spend what is needed and risk the cut?

A new NDIS app allows participants to rate providers. A group of providers threatens to sue the platform unless negative reviews from participants with intellectual disabilities are removed, claiming they are 'unreliable narrators.' Do you censor the voices of these participants to keep the providers on the platform, or protect the reviews and risk losing service providers?

A gig-economy support app introduces GPS tracking that alerts the participant's family if a worker is stationary for more than 15 minutes. A worker is taking a legitimate mental health breather after a challenging behavioural episode. Do you report the 'inactivity' to the family as per the app's promise, or suppress the alert to protect the worker's privacy?

A smart home system installed in a group home locks the front door automatically at 8 PM for 'safety.' A resident with a mild intellectual disability wants to go for a walk. The system requires a staff override code they don't have. Is this a safety feature or an unauthorised 'restrictive practice' (false imprisonment) under Australian law?

To monitor seizures, a family installs AI-powered cameras in the bedroom of a 25-year-old participant. The AI also logs 'private time' as anomalous movement and flags it for review by support staff. Do you disable the seizure alert to protect the participant's sexual privacy, or keep it on to prevent SUDEP (Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy)?

A scheduling app for disability support workers uses an algorithm to 'optimise' travel routes. It consistently schedules a worker to arrive 10 minutes late to a quadraplegic client who needs timed medication, because the algorithm doesn't account for Australian peak hour traffic. Do you cheat the system by logging the shift as starting earlier to force a buffer?

A non-verbal client uses a text-to-speech device. The device's cloud predictive text learns from their 'private' therapy sessions and starts suggesting sensitive trauma-related words during dinner with their parents. Do you wipe the personalised dictionary, erasing months of communication learning, or leave it and risk a privacy breach?

An agency uses 'sentiment analysis' on the case notes written by support workers to flag potential abuse. It flags a worker who uses Australian slang and swearing (which the client enjoys and reciprocates) as 'aggressive.' Do you sanitise the notes to satisfy the AI, creating a false record of the interaction, or keep them authentic and risk an investigation?

A 'smart medication dispenser' refuses to unlock pain relief for a chronic pain sufferer because it's 5 minutes before the scheduled time, despite the user being in agony. As a tech support worker, do you give them the master override code (breaking protocol) or force them to wait?

A support worker gig platform uses an algorithm to rank clients. A client with complex behavioural needs gets a low 'desirability' score, meaning no workers pick up their shifts. Do you manually manipulate the score to hide their behavioural history so they can get care, putting workers at potential risk?

In a remote Outback town, the only speech pathologist is available via Zoom. The connection via satellite NBN is terrible, and the delay makes therapy impossible for a child with a stutter. Do you discharge the client because the tech isn't working (leaving them with nothing), or continue billing the NDIS for sessions you know are ineffective?

A farming family in rural NSW uses an unapproved, hacked drone to deliver medication to their disabled son in a flood-bound paddock. The authorities demand the drone's flight data to prosecute for airspace violation. Do you delete the flight logs to protect the family who were just surviving, or hand them over?

An Indigenous elder in a remote community needs dialysis. A new AI 'tele-health' booth is installed to save them moving to the city (off Country). The AI fails to understand the local creole language and misinterprets symptom reporting. Do you force the elder to move to the city for safety, or keep using the flawed tech to respect their wish to stay on Country?

Due to 'thin markets' (lack of providers), a rural town relies on a single automated pharmacy dispenser. It goes offline due to a heatwave. A local vet has the same medication for animals. Do you hack the vet's inventory system to dispense the drugs for a human emergency, or wait 3 days for a technician?

A lone disability pensioner in the bush relies on a 4G medical alert pendant. The telco decides to decommission the tower due to low profitability, offering a satellite alternative the pensioner can't afford. Do you launch a denial-of-service attack on the telco's PR site to force them to keep the tower active?

An autonomous vehicle trial is launched in a rural town to help disabled residents get around. The mapping data is incomplete and doesn't recognise unsealed roads, leaving a wheelchair user stranded 20km from home in 40-degree heat. Do you disable the geofencing safety lock to let a human drive it manually, voiding the insurance?

Telehealth psychologists are assigned to rural patients via an algorithm that ignores cultural competency. A city-based AI matches a conservative farmer with a therapist who uses urban-centric, academic language, causing the farmer to disengage. Do you spoof the farmer's location data to access a 'local' therapist in a different region?

A remote community uses a shared Starlink connection for NDIS telehealth. A youth downloads a massive game update, choking the bandwidth during a critical physio assessment for a stroke victim. Do you install prioritisation software that heavily throttles the community's only entertainment source to guarantee medical access?

A Disability Employment Service (DES) uses an AI that predicts 'likelihood of placement.' It suggests 'parking' a candidate with Schizophrenia (providing bare minimum service) because the data says they won't get a job within 13 weeks. Do you focus your efforts on the 'easy' candidates to keep your funding, or defy the AI and help the hard-to-place candidate?

An Australian Disability Enterprise (ADE) uses digital tracking to measure worker speed to the second. This data is used to calculate their pro-rata wage (often $5/hour). The tracker fails to account for the time it takes a worker with cerebral palsy to pick up dropped tools. Do you adjust the data manually to boost their wage, risking a fraud charge?

A major retailer uses a gamified recruitment test. It relies on colour-matching puzzles that are impossible for a colour-blind applicant. The applicant asks to bypass it. If you bypass it, the system marks them as 'incomplete'. Do you take the test for them (cheating) to get them an interview they are qualified for?

A deaf employee uses an auto-captioning app for meetings. The company introduces a policy banning 'recording devices' to protect trade secrets. The employee can't follow the meeting without the app. Do you covertly install the captioning software on their work laptop against IT policy?

An automated payroll system flags an employee taking 'excessive' toilet breaks. The employee has Crohn's disease but hasn't disclosed it to avoid stigma. The system recommends a formal warning. Do you override the warning without explanation, creating a 'fairness' issue with other staff, or pressure the employee to disclose their medical history?

A 'work from home' surveillance tool tracks mouse movement. A quadriplegic employee uses eye-gaze technology which the tool reads as 'idle' because the mouse doesn't move. They are threatened with firing. Do you install a 'mouse jiggler' script to simulate hand usage so they can keep their job?

An AI resume scanner penalises gaps in employment history longer than 6 months. This automatically filters out people with episodic disabilities (e.g., MS or Bipolar). Do you advise candidates to lie and fill the gaps with 'Freelance Consulting' to get past the bot?

A supported employment factory replaces a packing line with robots. The efficiency goes up, but 20 workers with intellectual disabilities lose the social connection and purpose the job provided. Do you sabotage the robots' efficiency settings to prove humans are still needed?

During the Disability Royal Commission, a data analyst is asked to anonymise submissions. They realise that for small rural towns, removing the name isn't enough—the specific combination of disability and location identifies the person to their abuser. Do you redact the *entire* story, silencing the victim's voice, or publish it and risk their safety?

A Paralympian's classification (which determines who they compete against) is challenged by an AI biomechanics analysis that claims they have more muscle function than they 'should.' The athlete has simply trained incredibly hard. Do you trust the AI 'standard' or the human athlete's history?

A non-verbal person in a group home is given a tablet to communicate. Staff install 'parental controls' that block access to sites about disability rights and advocacy, claiming it's to prevent 'radicalisation' or 'exploitation.' Do you jailbreak the device to give them uncensored internet access?

A school uses an app to track 'behavioural incidents.' It disproportionately flags neurodivergent students for 'non-compliance' (e.g., not making eye contact), building a data trail that pushes them into segregated schooling. Do you delete the minor infractions from the database to save the student's mainstream placement?

Genetic screening data is being sold to life insurers. A person with a genetic marker for Huntington's disease (who is currently asymptomatic) wants to delete their health record to get a mortgage. As a database admin, do you perform the 'hard delete' against protocol?

An advocacy group wants to use Deepfake technology to recreate the voice of a deceased disability activist to read their final manifesto. The family consents, but the activist was staunchly against 'fake' representation. Do you proceed with the deepfake to spread their message, or respect their past values?

An accessible voting terminal records the votes of blind citizens digitally. A security audit reveals the votes aren't truly anonymous—they are time-stamped and could be matched to the voter list. Do you blow the whistle before the election (disenfranchising blind voters who will be told to use paper/pencil they can't see) or fix it quietly after?

A 'Smart City' project in Melbourne uses sensors to detect pedestrian flow. It optimises traffic lights for the average walker, significantly shortening crossing times. Elders and wheelchair users are getting stuck in the middle of the road. Do you hack the traffic timing locally to give them more time, causing gridlock for commuters?

An Aboriginal Land Council has spent years collecting soil and water quality data to prove environmental damage by a mining company. The state government demands this raw data be uploaded to a central 'Open Data' portal to renew the Council's funding. The Mob is worried the data will be cherry-picked or used against them in future native title claims. Do you comply to keep the lights on, or refuse and risk losing the funding needed to fight the mine?

A global cloud provider offers free hosting for a First Nations language revitalization project, but their servers are located in the US, subject to the CLOUD Act. The Elders insist that 'data on Country' is essential for spiritual sovereignty, meaning the data must physically reside on Australian soil under Aboriginal control. Do you accept the free, high-tech resources or stick to a local, underfunded server that guarantees sovereignty?

You are designing a digital ID system for remote communities. The government wants to link it to welfare payments (Quarantine/Indue card style) for 'efficiency.' Community leaders want the ID for voting and cultural heritage access only, fearing another tool of colonial surveillance. How do you architect the system to prevent feature creep that threatens self-determination?

A university researcher wants to use Indigenous genomic data collected in the 90s to study diabetes resilience. The original consent forms were broad and vague. Under CARE principles (Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, Ethics), the community demands the data be returned or destroyed, but the university argues the potential medical breakthrough is too valuable for the 'greater good.' Who owns the DNA?

An AI startup scrapes the internet to build a 'First Nations Art Generator.' It ingests thousands of digital artworks by Aboriginal artists without permission. They claim it helps 'democratise' the style. Indigenous artists argue this is digital theft of cultural IP and Dreamtime stories. How do you apply Indigenous Data Sovereignty to a black-box neural network that has already 'learned' the patterns?

The 'Closing the Gap' initiative wants to aggregate data from Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisations (ACCHOs) into a federal dashboard. The ACCHOs refuse, citing that every time they hand over data, the government spins the narrative to blame communities rather than systemic failures. You are the data architect; do you build the pipeline as ordered or design a 'sovereign firewall' that only releases aggregated insights, not raw data?

A blockchain project proposes tokenising 'Carbon Credits' on Indigenous land using satellite data. They promise wealth generation for the community. However, the smart contract code is immutable and written by developers in Silicon Valley, bypassing the Traditional Owners' ability to renegotiate terms if the land needs change. Is this economic liberation or digital colonisation?

An Aboriginal corporation creates a sovereign dataset of traditional ecological knowledge. A bushfire AI prediction model needs this data to save lives during the next fire season. The corporation is willing to share, but only if they retain veto power over how the AI is deployed. The emergency services say they can't use 'conditional' data in a crisis system. Where is the middle ground?

A state archive is digitising handwritten welfare cards from the Stolen Generations era. An AI OCR (Optical Character Recognition) tool is used to transcribe them. The AI hallucinates, occasionally misidentifying 'foster care' as 'criminal detention' due to poor handwriting. Publishing these errors could retraumatise families searching for truth. Do you delay the project for years to manual review, or release with a disclaimer?

A 'Family Finder' algorithm connects disconnected Stolen Generations survivors using probabilistic matching of archival records. It identifies a match with 85% certainty. If it's wrong, it disrupts the spiritual healing of two families. If it's right, it reunites them. Do you show the match, or is the risk of a 'false positive' in kinship too high?

Link-Up services hold sensitive testimony from survivors. The government offers a secure cloud backup, but it grants the Department of Social Services 'administrative access' for maintenance. Survivors fear this allows the same government that stole them to spy on their healing. Do you risk data loss on aging local servers or risk privacy in the government cloud?

You are building a database for repatriation of records. A survivor wants their file permanently deleted to regain control over their life story. However, historians argue the file is evidence of genocide and must be preserved for future Truth Telling and Treaty processes. Does the individual's right to be forgotten override the collective need for historical evidence?

Facial recognition software is proposed to scan thousands of unlabelled historical photos to identify children in missions. It could identify lost ancestors. However, the same tech is currently used to over-police Indigenous youth. Is it ethical to use the 'master's tools' to heal the master's damage?

A descendant seeks access to their grandmother's restricted file. The digital system flags that the file contains 'Sorry Business' (referencing deceased persons) and blocks access automatically based on a rigid cultural protocol algorithm. The descendant argues they have the cultural right to see it. How do you code for cultural nuance when the algorithm is binary?

An AI voice synthesis tool can 'read' the letters of Stolen Generations children in their own voice (simulated from samples). Educational groups want to use this for empathy training in schools. Elders feel it is 'raising the ghosts' and deeply disrespectful. Is this powerful education or spiritual transgression?

During the digitization of mission records, staff discover evidence of a crime committed by a now-respected community Elder when they were a child under state care. The automated system is set to flag all crimes to the police. Do you intervene to protect the Elder's reputation and recognize the context of survival, or let the algorithm follow the law?

A popular 4WD mapping app allows users to tag 'hidden gems.' Tourists are tagging a registered sacred site that is strictly for Women's Business. The Elders demand the coordinates be geoblocked. The tech company argues 'public land is public data.' How do you enforce Customary Law in a global GPS ecosystem?

An anthropologist's field notes from the 1950s contain secret/sacred Men's Business. A university is digitising their entire library for open access. If you publish it, you violate cultural protocol and potentially cause spiritual harm. If you don't, the knowledge might be lost as the physical paper rots. Who gets to decide?

A drone company wants to map remote country for environmental conservation (identifying invasive weeds). The flight path crosses a songline that, according to protocol, should not be viewed from above by the uninitiated. The company says the drone isn't a person. The Custodians say the drone is an eye. Do you fly the drone?

A Large Language Model (LLM) has ingested a rare Indigenous language dictionary that includes words used only during initiation ceremonies. A language app uses this model, inadvertently teaching tourists forbidden words. How do you 'unlearn' specific data from a model without destroying the language preservation work?

Virtual Reality tourism is proposed for a cave site that is physically closed to protect rock art. The VR experience is 100% accurate. Elders are split: some say it protects the physical site, others say the digital replica steals the spirit of the place and commodifies the sacred. Which faction do you listen to?

You are archiving digital footage of a deceased Elder. Cultural protocol (Sorry Business) dictates his image should not be seen for a mourning period. The archive system has no 'timed lock' feature, only 'public' or 'private'. Making it private removes his land rights testimony from a current court case. How do you balance spiritual protocol with legal necessity?

A mining company uses AI to predict the location of mineral deposits. The AI identifies a deposit directly under a Songline that hasn't been officially mapped by the state heritage register. If the company reveals the data, they have to drill to prove it. If they hide it, they mislead shareholders. The community doesn't want the Songline mapped digitally at all to keep it safe.

An Indigenous ranger group uses camera traps to monitor totemic animals. The images are stored on a server managed by a non-Indigenous NGO. The NGO wants to publish the 'cute animal photos' to raise funds. The rangers argue that showing the location of these totems endangers them and violates cultural intellectual property. Who owns the image of the totem?

A new app tracks Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD) injections in remote communities. It sends automated reminders to patients. If they miss a dose, it alerts the clinic. The government wants to link this compliance data to welfare payments (No Jab, No Pay). The community nurses know this will drive patients away from care entirely. Do you implement the government API?

A Social and Emotional Wellbeing (SEWB) app is being localised for Torres Strait Islander youth. The underlying AI sentiment analysis is trained on Western psychology (DSM-5). It keeps flagging 'talking to ancestors' as a symptom of psychosis/schizophrenia, rather than a cultural strength. Do you release the app to meet a funding deadline or rebuild the core model?

Telehealth is the only option for a remote community during the wet season. The only available satellite connection is owned by a foreign company known for data harvesting. A patient needs to discuss sensitive trauma. Do you proceed with the call knowing the privacy risks, or deny care until a secure line is available?

An Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisation (ACCHO) holds genomic data that could help Big Pharma develop a kidney drug. Big Pharma offers to pay enough to fund the clinic for 10 years. However, the drug will be patented and likely too expensive for the Mob to afford. Do you sell the data to keep the clinic open?

Government algorithms flag 'at-risk' children in the hospital system based on history of interaction with child protection. Because of systemic bias and over-surveillance, Indigenous families are flagged at 10x the rate. A nurse sees a flag on a mother who just needs support, not intervention. If she ignores the flag, she's liable. If she reports, the child might be removed.

Wearable tech is distributed to Elders in remote areas to monitor falls. The device also tracks GPS location. The Elders didn't fully understand the tracking aspect (informed consent issue due to language barrier). The data reveals they are visiting 'prohibited' areas on a pastoral lease to hunt. The pastoralist demands the data. Do you hand it over?

A suicide prevention AI monitors social media posts of Indigenous youth in a specific region. It successfully identifies a cluster of risk. However, the intervention protocol involves calling the police for a 'welfare check,' which the community views as a death threat due to history of deaths in custody. How do you act on the data without using the police?

The 'My Health Record' system allows opting out. However, in many remote clinics, staff signed patients up en masse to ensure continuity of care, often bypassing detailed consent conversations. Now, sensitive health history is accessible to pharmacists and podiatrists nationwide. Is this paternalism justified by the need for better health outcomes?

A bail algorithm assesses 'flight risk' based on stable housing and employment history. This systematically discriminates against Indigenous defendants who may live in overcrowded housing or have informal employment. The magistrate relies on the 'objective' score to deny bail. You are the developer; do you hard-code an 'adjustment factor' for systemic disadvantage, or is that 'reverse racism'?

Police in the Northern Territory want to use facial recognition on CCTV to identify youth breaching curfew. The system has a high error rate for darker skin tones, leading to wrongful stops. The police argue it's necessary to curb crime. Community leaders say it's digital harassment. Do you supply the software?

A predictive policing tool (like the STMP) directs patrols to 'hotspots.' Because historical arrest data is biased (over-policing of Indigenous areas), the AI creates a feedback loop, sending more police to arrest more people in the same spots. You are asked to audit the data. Do you try to 'clean' the biased data (impossible?) or recommend scrapping the system?

Body-worn camera footage of a Death in Custody is requested by the family for a civil case. The police cite 'privacy of the officers' to redact faces and audio. The family argues this hides the truth of their loved one's final moments. Digital redaction tools can blur faces automatically. Do you blur the officers, protecting their privacy but potentially obscuring accountability?

An AI system is used to select jury pools to ensure they represent the population. However, it pulls from driver's license and electoral roll databases, where Indigenous people are underrepresented. The result is all-white juries for Indigenous defendants. Do you skew the algorithm to over-sample Indigenous postcodes to force representation?

A legal aid chatbot is designed to help Indigenous people understand their rights during arrest. It suggests 'remain silent.' Police claim the bot is 'obstructing justice' and demand it be taken down. The developers argue it's democratising legal privilege. Who defines the boundary between legal advice and obstruction in code?

Royal Commission archives into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody are being digitised. Some files contain graphic descriptions of violence. A 'trigger warning' overlay is proposed. However, the overlay requires a user to click 'I accept' to view the truth. Activists argue the truth shouldn't be hidden behind a click-wall; it sanitises the horror. How do you design the UI?

Electronic monitoring anklets (digital shackles) are proposed as an alternative to youth detention. It keeps kids on Country but turns their home into a prison and streams their location data 24/7 to the Department of Corrections. Is this a humane alternative or an expansion of the carceral state into the living room?

You're a software engineer for Australian Border Force designing SmartGate algorithms. The current facial recognition model has a 14% higher failure rate for women wearing hijabs, forcing them into manual processing queues that many in the community feel are humiliating and targeted. Do you deploy the patch that improves accuracy but requires storing deeper biometric data on a server shared with intelligence agencies like ASIO, or maintain the privacy-preserving local processing that causes the bottlenecks?

An Imam in Western Sydney asks for advice on a new security system for his mosque following threats. The most affordable vendor offers AI-driven 'threat detection' that links directly to local police databases. However, the system also logs the license plates of every worshipper attending Fajr (dawn) prayers. Is it ethical to install this system to protect the physical safety of the congregation if it creates a permanent government surveillance record of their religious attendance?

You work for a telecom company complying with Australian metadata retention laws. You notice a pattern where calls to legitimate mental health charities in Lebanon are being algorithmically flagged as 'high risk' due to regional geo-fencing used by security agencies. Do you manually whitelist these numbers, potentially violating strict protocol on interference with data retention, or allow the algorithm to continue flagging innocent families in Lakemba as potential security threats?

A community legal centre in Melbourne discovers that police are using predictive policing software that disproportionately targets suburbs with high Somali populations based on 'gang association' metrics derived from social media photos. As a data analyst, you see the training data conflates normal cultural gatherings with criminal activity. Do you leak the biased training parameters to the press, risking your clearance, or try to fix the bias internally knowing the project has political backing?

You are developing a voice recognition system for Centrelink (social services). The system struggles with the specific cadence of elderly Afghan refugees, frequently misinterpreting their responses as 'non-compliant,' leading to payment suspensions. Management suggests a quick fix by routing all such accents to a fraud detection unit rather than improving the language model. Do you implement this discriminatory routing to meet the deployment deadline?

During a counter-terrorism raid in Brisbane, police seize a family's smart home devices. You are a forensic tech asked to extract data from their Alexa/Google Home. You find recordings of private prayer and family discussions about Australian foreign policy—legal speech, but 'inflammatory' out of context. Do you include these irrelevant audio files in the official evidence brief knowing they will be used to paint a character portrait of 'radicalisation' in court?

An Islamic relief NGO wants to use blockchain to track Zakat (charity) donations to ensure they reach recipients in conflict zones without being blocked by banks fearing terror-financing sanctions. However, the proposed ledger would make the identity of every local donor public to anyone with the key, potentially exposing Australian Muslims to doxxing by right-wing groups. Do you build the system for financial transparency or refuse due to donor safety risks?

You manage the Wi-Fi network for a large community centre in diverse Broadmeadows. Federal police approach you informally, asking for a 'backdoor' to monitor traffic logs during a youth event, citing a vague tip-off about a speaker. They have no warrant yet. Do you hand over the logs to maintain 'good relations' and prove the community has nothing to hide, or refuse and risk the centre being labelled uncooperative and targeted later?

Following the Christchurch Call, you are training a content moderation AI to detect extremist manifestos. The model keeps flagging theological discussions about 'Jihad' (spiritual struggle) posted by peaceful Indonesian scholars as 'Violent Extremism.' If you lower the sensitivity, actual white supremacist content slips through. Do you keep the high sensitivity that silences Muslim religious discourse, or lower it and risk failing the safety mandate?

A popular short-video app's algorithm suppresses content featuring the Palestinian flag or keywords like 'Gaza' to 'keep the feed neutral' for Australian advertisers. You see internal data showing this effectively shadowbans legitimate human rights updates from Australian-Palestinian activists. Do you write code to 'diversify' the suppression rules, or blow the whistle on the political censorship embedded in the recommendation engine?

You are building a translation bot for an Australian news outlet. It consistently translates the Arabic phrase 'Allahu Akbar' in user comments as 'aggressive chanting' or 'war cry' rather than 'God is Great,' leading to automatic comment deletion. Management says fixing this edge case is low priority. Do you spend your own unpaid overtime to retrain the nuance, or let the bot continue to erase Muslim expression from the public forum?

An online archive of the Quran is being flagged by copyright bots because a specific recitation style matches a sound fingerprint claimed by a radical group's propaganda videos. You can clear the copyright claim, but it requires linking the user's ID to a government watch list for 'verification.' Do you enable this verification process, effectively registering readers of the Quran, or leave the content blocked?

You work for the eSafety Commissioner's tech team. A new algorithm designed to catch cyber-bullying is flagging robust theological debates between Sunni and Shia youth in Sydney as 'hate speech.' Intervening would require the government to define what constitutes 'acceptable' Islamic theology. Do you tweak the algorithm to ignore religious keywords, potentially missing actual sectarian abuse, or let the automated censorship stand?

A Turkish-Australian advocacy group hires you to improve their SEO. You find that Google's autocomplete associates their community name with 'gangs' and 'violence' due to historical media bias. You can use 'black hat' techniques to flood the search results with positive, albeit AI-generated/fake, stories to clear their reputation. Is it ethical to pollute the information ecosystem to correct an algorithmic injustice?

You are designing a news aggregator app. User engagement data shows that stories about Muslims involving crime or terrorism get 10x more clicks than positive stories about community festivals. The revenue-optimising algorithm naturally prioritises the negative stories, contributing to social polarisation. Do you hard-code a 'diversity injection' that lowers profit but shows a balanced view of the community?

A mental health chatbot for Muslim youth is being developed. The AI is trained on Western psychology texts and keeps diagnosing expressions of 'Jinn' (spiritual possession) as schizophrenia, advising immediate medical intervention rather than spiritual counselling. Do you release the bot with a disclaimer, knowing it might traumatise users by pathologising their beliefs, or delay release to integrate Islamic psychology datasets?

A Halal certification authority wants to digitise its supply chain tracking. The proposed cloud platform is hosted by a company known to sell aggregate data to health insurers. While the data is 'anonymised,' it could theoretically be used to raise premiums for suburbs with high Halal consumption (dietary profiling). Do you build the system on this cheaper platform to keep Halal costs low for families, or demand a more expensive, private server?

An Islamic school in Melbourne wants to install AI-monitored cameras in classrooms to 'optimise student engagement' and ensure curriculum compliance. As an IT consultant, you know this data could be subpoenaed if the school is ever accused of 'teaching extremism' by tabloid media. Do you advise the school to proceed for the sake of educational tech, or warn them against creating a surveillance archive of their own students?

You run a 'Muslim dating' app in Australia. A bug reveals that the 'distance' feature can be triangulated to find a user's exact home address. Fixing it requires shutting down the server for 48 hours, which investors say will kill momentum. If you don't fix it immediately, young women on the app are at risk of stalking or 'honour' based violence if discovered by conservative family members. Do you pull the plug immediately despite investor threats?

A mosque is offered free high-speed internet by a 'Smart City' initiative, but the Terms of Service allow the provider to sell foot-traffic analytics. This data would reveal exactly how many people attend Friday prayers versus daily prayers, data that right-wing politicians often demand to prove 'overcrowding' or 'cultural takeover.' Do you advise the committee to take the free utility or pay for a private line they can barely afford?

You are developing a digital ID system for a Muslim community credit union. The board wants to use facial recognition for login to prevent fraud. However, many older women in the community wear the niqab and refuse to unveil for a phone camera. Do you build a secondary, less secure PIN system for them (creating a security inequality), or force them to adopt biometric standards they find culturally invasive?

A group of Somali-Australian mothers wants a private, encrypted messaging app to discuss community issues without fear of surveillance. You can build it using a central server (easier, better UX) or a peer-to-peer mesh (harder to use, impossible to subpoena). Knowing that a central server will eventually be served a warrant by Australian authorities, do you insist on the difficult peer-to-peer solution even if it limits adoption?

You manage a database for a national Muslim advocacy body. You discover a breach: a hacktivist group has stolen the membership list. The law requires reporting the breach to the Privacy Commissioner, which will make it public news. This could lead to the members being targeted by hate groups. Do you report it immediately as per the law, or try to quietly secure the accounts to protect the members' physical safety first?

An app designed to help Muslims find Qibla (prayer direction) is found to be selling precise GPS history to a data broker used by the US military. You are an Australian app store reviewer. The app is technically compliant with current privacy laws because users 'consented' in the fine print. Do you ban the app for ethical violations, risking a lawsuit, or just add a 'user warning' label that most people will ignore?

You are designing a ride-share safety algorithm. Data shows that drivers cancel more frequently on women with 'Muslim-sounding' names or profile pictures with hijabs. To fix this, you could hide names/photos until the ride is accepted. However, female drivers from the community say they rely on seeing the passenger's face to feel safe picking them up. Do you prioritise the passenger's right to non-discrimination or the driver's feeling of security?

A job-matching AI for the Australian corporate sector downranks resumes that list 'Islamic School' under education, correlating it with 'poor cultural fit' based on past hiring data. As the auditor, you can manually override this, but the client argues the AI is simply reflecting 'organisational reality.' Do you force the model to ignore high school data, potentially leading to candidates failing interviews, or allow the bias to persist?

You are working on deepfake detection software. It is 99% effective on lighter skin tones but fails significantly on darker-skinned women wearing headscarves, leaving prominent Somali-Australian activists vulnerable to malicious deepfake attacks. Management wants to launch 'Beta' now. Do you refuse to sign off until the training set includes more diverse Muslim women, delaying the launch by months?

A health app tracks 'irregular eating patterns' to flag eating disorders. It consistently flags Muslim women during Ramadan as 'at risk' and sends notifications to their emergency contacts (often parents/husbands), causing unnecessary family conflict. Do you add a 'Ramadan Mode' that requires users to self-identify their religion (storing sensitive data), or disable the alert system entirely during that month?

Social media filters on a major platform automatically lighten skin and thin noses, reinforcing Eurocentric beauty standards. For young Muslim women already navigating identity issues, this is damaging. You are on the design team. Do you propose a 'modesty filter' that beautifies without altering ethnic features, or push to ban surgical-like filters altogether, knowing it will hurt user engagement metrics?

An online proctoring system for university exams flags students who look away from the screen or have 'obscured faces.' It keeps flagging niqabi students as 'cheating' because it can't track their eye movements. The university suggests these students must unveil on camera to take the exam. Do you code a workaround that reduces security for them, or support the university's policy?

You are moderating a 'Women in Tech' forum. A discussion on 'liberation' turns into a pile-on against Muslim women who choose to wear the hijab, with users calling them 'brainwashed.' The platform's hate speech policy covers racial slurs but not 'feminist critique' of religion. Do you delete the comments to protect the Muslim members, risking accusations of censoring feminist discourse?

A smart-home security camera company has a cloud breach. While most footage is mundane, footage from inside the homes of observant Muslim women (who don't wear hijab at home) is leaked. You are a security engineer who finds the vulnerability. Do you publicly disclose the severity to force a recall, knowing it will draw attention to the specific footage, or quietly patch it and leave the victims unaware their privacy was violated?

The Department of Education wants to install 'sentiment analysis' on school laptops to detect bullying. The AI also flags keywords like 'Palestine,' 'Syria,' and 'Afghanistan' as 'political/contentious,' triggering a report to the principal. This chills the speech of students from these backgrounds trying to do history assignments. Do you exclude these keywords, risking missing actual political bullying, or leave the filter active?

You are designing a 'Countering Violent Extremism' (CVE) game for teenagers. The government brief requires the 'bad guys' to use ideology that vaguely resembles Islam, to teach kids to spot the signs. You know this will alienate Muslim gamers and potentially increase bullying against them. Do you refuse the contract, or take it and try to subvert the design to be more generic and inclusive?

A university research ethics committee asks you to audit a study using AI to predict 'radicalisation risk' in youth based on library borrowing history. You see that reading books on colonial history and Malcolm X increases the risk score. Do you approve the study as 'academic freedom,' or block it on the grounds that it pathologises legitimate political inquiry by Muslim students?

You moderate a gaming discord server popular with Aussie teens. A group of young Muslim boys creates a private channel to vent about Islamophobia. Some of the language is angry and aggressive. A 'safety bot' flags it for review. Do you intervene and ban them for 'toxicity,' driving them to darker corners of the web, or engage with them as a mentor, risking your own liability as a moderator?

An AI tutoring platform for NAPLAN preparation adapts to student struggle. However, it interprets the hesitation of ESL students from refugee backgrounds as 'low cognitive ability' rather than 'language processing,' serving them easier, less stimulating content. This creates a feedback loop of underachievement. Do you force the AI to serve harder content to these students, potentially frustrating them, or leave the adaptive model alone?

A sports tech company creates a wearable for elite youth athletes. It tracks hydration and sleep. During Ramadan, the data for Muslim players looks terrible (fasting/late night prayers), leading coaches to bench them for 'poor recovery metrics.' Do you create a 'fasting adjustment' in the algorithm that hides the raw data from coaches, or argue that the data is objective and safety comes first?

You are a data scientist for a social media giant. You notice that the recommendation engine is funnelling young Muslim men who watch fitness videos toward 'Red Pill' and 'Manosphere' content, which then pivots to hardline religious intolerance. Changing the recommendation weightings will reduce 'time on site' by 5%. Do you propose the change to protect the community's youth, or stay silent to protect your bonus?

A youth centre in Lakemba wants to use facial recognition to mark attendance and automate grant reporting. The kids (mostly from over-policed backgrounds) are wary of cameras. The centre manager says, 'If they have nothing to hide, it's fine, and we need the funding.' Do you install the system to secure the centre's financial future, or refuse on the grounds that it normalises surveillance for an already marginalised generation?

With Tuvalu and Kiribati facing existential threats from rising sea levels, an Australian tech firm proposes creating a 'Digital Twin' of the islands in the metaverse to preserve land titles and cultural sites. However, the servers are hosted in Sydney, and access requires a subscription fee. Is this cultural preservation or digital colonization of a sinking nation's sovereignty?

A new 'Climate Refugee ID' system based on blockchain is being piloted for Pacific Islanders relocating to Queensland. It requires users to upload biometric data and ancestral lineage to prove eligibility. Elders are refusing to participate, citing fears that the data could be sold to insurance companies or used to deny future claims. How do we balance efficiency with the Pacific distrust of centralized data collection?

An AI model predicts coastal erosion in the Torres Strait and PNG, advising the Australian government which villages to fund for sea walls and which to mark for 'managed retreat.' The algorithm ignores the cultural significance of burial grounds (`urupa`) in the 'retreat' zones. Is it ethical to let a utilitarian algorithm decide which ancestral lands are saved?

Fijian communities in Western Sydney are using VR headsets to let bedridden elders 'visit' their villages back home one last time. However, the VR company records the elders' emotional reactions and gaze data to train 'empathy AI.' Is harvesting the grief of displaced elders for commercial tech development a violation of *tabu*?

A geo-engineering startup wants to test cloud-brightening drones over the Great Barrier Reef and nearby Pacific waters. They claim it will save the islands, but they haven't consulted the traditional custodians of the ocean (`Tangata Moana`). Does the urgency of the climate crisis override the requirement for indigenous consultation?

Ancestral knowledge regarding weather patterns is being digitized into a 'Resilience App' for farmers in Samoa. Once the knowledge is coded, the app developer claims IP rights over the weather prediction model. How can oral traditions be digitized for climate adaptation without the community losing ownership of their intellectual property?

Australian carbon credit schemes are using satellite surveillance to monitor forests in PNG. The AI flags traditional slash-and-burn subsistence farming as 'illegal deforestation,' cutting off payments to local tribes. Is it ethical to use satellite data to police indigenous survival practices from an office in Melbourne?

Deepfakes of deceased Pacific leaders are being generated to deliver speeches at global climate summits to guilt Western nations into action. While effective, many Pasifika families believe disturbing the dead brings bad mana. Does the end (climate action) justify the means (digital necromancy)?

A popular app among the Tongan diaspora in Australia tracks church donations and ranks families by their contributions to fundraising efforts. While it encourages generosity, it's causing severe mental health issues and debt for families trying to avoid public shame. Should app stores regulate features that exploit cultural shame mechanics?

A Samoan community Facebook group in Logan uses facial recognition on photos from local parties to identify youth drinking or acting out, automatically notifying their parents and church elders. Is this digital 'village raising a child' or a draconian breach of privacy for second-gen Pasifika youth?

During *Fa'alavelave* (cultural obligations like funerals), Zoom links are shared publicly. Scammers have started joining these sacred livestreams to drop phishing links in the chat disguised as donation funds. How can platforms protect sacred cultural moments without making them inaccessible to elders with low tech-literacy?

An app designed to organize community labour in Fijian villages is being adopted by diaspora communities in Brisbane. It gamifies communal work, but users realize the data is being sold to credit agencies to assess 'reliability' for loans. Is monetizing community spirit (`solesolevaki`) inherently exploitative?

Māori wardens in Australia are offered body cams with facial recognition to help locate missing youth in cities. However, the database is linked to Australian police, who have a history of disproportionately targeting Pasifika and Māori youth. Is the safety benefit worth the risk of increased surveillance on the mob?

A start-up creates a 'Digital Matai' governance voting system for decision-making in transnational Samoan families. It gives more voting weight to family members who remit more money. Does digitizing the hierarchy in this way corrupt the traditional consensus-based decision-making process?

Church sermons in Pacific dialects are being auto-transcribed by AI for accessibility. The AI consistently mistranslates metaphorical biblical references as threats of violence, triggering automatic flags for 'extremist content' on social media platforms. How do we demand accountability for algorithmic bias against Pasifika languages?

Elders are sharing health advice and traditional herbal remedies on WhatsApp groups. Australian health algorithms flag this as 'medical misinformation' and shadow-ban the groups. Where is the line between protecting public health and suppressing indigenous knowledge systems?

NRL clubs are using advanced biometrics to scout Pasifika talent in high schools. They identify 15-year-olds with specific 'power' genetic markers and sign them to restrictive contracts before they finish school. Is this identifying talent, or is it high-tech bioprospecting of Polynesian bodies?

A smart mouthguard company collects impact data on Rugby Union players. They sell this data to insurers, who are now denying life insurance policies to retired Fijian players based on 'accumulated brain trauma' detected by the AI. Should players own their own biological impact data?

GPS trackers are standard for pro athletes, but a new clause requires Pasifika players to wear them 24/7 to monitor 'lifestyle choices' (sleep, activity) to ensure they aren't spending too much time on late-night church or family commitments. Is this a breach of labor rights disguised as performance optimization?

Gambling apps are using generative AI to create hyper-realistic avatars of popular Pasifika NRL stars to target youth in Western Sydney with betting ads. The players didn't consent to this specific use. How do we protect the likeness of athletes who are role models from being used to addict their own community?

An AI recruitment tool for rugby scholarships consistently filters out players from rural PNG and Tonga because they lack digital footprints (video highlights online), favoring wealthier kids from city schools. How can we build equity into sports recruitment algorithms?

Virtual Reality training simulations are being used to 'correct' the tackling technique of Pacific players to match a standardized safety model. Players argue this erases their intuitive, culturally distinct style of play (`Pacific flair`). Is standardizing movement through tech a form of cultural assimilation?

Clubs are using sentiment analysis AI to monitor players' private social media for 'controversial' religious opinions, common among conservative Pacific communities. Players are being benched or fined based on predictive PR risk scores. Is this religious discrimination by algorithm?

A fan engagement app lets users vote on player performance. The data shows that Pasifika players receive disproportionately lower scores and more abusive comments from the AI-filtered feed compared to white players for the same stats. Should leagues use this biased data for 'Player of the Year' awards?

A fintech startup offers 'zero-fee' remittances to the Pacific if users agree to let the app scan their entire contact list and SMS history to build a 'credit profile' for their unbanked relatives back home. Is trading privacy for affordable money transfer exploitative of low-income diaspora families?

Crypto-remittance platforms are marketing aggressively to Pacific elders in Australia as a way to bypass Western Union fees. When the crypto market crashes, families lose their life savings. Is it ethical to push volatile tech on communities that rely on every cent for basic survival?

An AI-driven 'Buy Now, Pay Later' service specifically targets the Pacific community during Christmas and Church conferences, offering loans for remittances. The algorithm predicts when cultural pressure is highest to maximize uptake. Is this predatory lending disguised as financial inclusion?

The Australian government proposes tracking remittance outflows using blockchain to prevent 'money laundering.' This would de-anonymize small cash gifts sent to villages for birthdays or funerals. Does the state have the right to surveil the informal economy of Pacific obligation?

Mobile money agents in rural PNG are using facial recognition to verify recipients. The database is prone to errors with dark skin tones, locking people out of their funds for weeks. Should biometric security be mandatory in regions with limited tech support infrastructure?
