A budgeting app advises Pasifika users to cut 'non-essential' spending. It categorizes remittances and church donations as 'discretionary entertainment,' lowering their financial wellness score and mortgage eligibility. How do we code cultural values into financial algorithms?

Scammers are using voice-cloning AI to mimic relatives in the islands, calling Australian family members in panic demanding immediate transfer of funds for 'emergencies.' The emotional manipulation exploits the deep Pasifika duty to care for family. How can telcos protect against this specific cultural vulnerability?

A new platform allows direct payment of utility bills in the islands from Australia. While convenient, it disempowers the local relatives by removing their agency to manage the cash sent, creating a dynamic of 'digital paternalism.' Does tech efficiency undermine family trust?

A major AI company scrapes the internet to build a Samoan language model. They include sacred oral histories and chiefly genealogies that were never meant for public consumption. Who owns the copyright to the 'Pacific Internet'—the platforms or the people?

An automated translation tool for hospitals in Auckland and Sydney translates Tongan accurately but fails to use the correct 'honorific' language levels for elders and royals. This causes offense and leads to patients disengaging from care. Is 'good enough' AI dangerous in high-context cultures?

To preserve the dying dialects of the Cook Islands, researchers want to record the last fluent speakers 24/7 using smart home devices. The elders agree, but don't understand that the data will be owned by the university, not their tribe. Is informed consent possible when the technology is foreign to the subjects?

Young Pasifika kids in Australia are learning their mother tongues via gamified apps like Duolingo. Elders complain the apps teach a 'colonized' version of the language that lacks the spiritual depth (*wairua*) of learning from a grandparent. Is imperfect digital preservation better than extinction?

Voice assistants (Siri/Alexa) struggle with Pasifika accents and names, forcing users to code-switch or anglicize their names to be understood. Parents worry this reinforces the idea that their natural way of speaking is 'incorrect.' Should tech companies be mandated to train on diverse local accents?

A generative AI art tool is being used to create 'traditional' Māori and Polynesian tattoo designs for tourists. It mixes symbols from different tribes and ranks indiscriminately. Is this AI-generated cultural appropriation, and does it devalue the role of the traditional tattoo master (*Tufuga*)?

Content moderation bots on TikTok frequently ban the use of the word 'coconut' by Pacific users discussing their own culture, labeling it as hate speech, while allowing actual abuse to slide. How do we teach AI the nuance of re-appropriated slurs within the community?

A funded project digitizes Fijian oral traditions into a chatbot so diaspora youth can 'ask an elder.' If the chatbot hallucinates (makes up fake stories), it corrupts the oral history chain permanently. Is the risk of AI hallucination too high for preserving sacred history?

An AI photo restoration tool is automatically colouring and animating historical archival photos in Alice Springs. However, it's inadvertently animating images of deceased Elders, violating strict 'Sorry Business' cultural protocols which forbid viewing images of the dead. Should the developers hard-code a 'cultural block' based on facial recognition, or is that an even greater invasion of privacy for the mob?

A remote community art centre in the APY Lands finds their dot painting styles are being scraped by a generative AI to create 'authentic style' Aboriginal art for tourist tea towels. The algorithm argues it's 'learning style', not copying specific works. How do we enforce Indigenous Cultural IP when the thief is a neural network hosted overseas?

Tourists are using Augmented Reality (AR) glasses at Uluru that overlay digital information. Some developers want to include 'secret men's business' stories historically recorded by anthropologists but strictly forbidden for uninitiated eyes. Is digital censorship required to protect the sanctity of the Songlines?

A translation app is being deployed in Central Australian courts to help judges understand Arrernte and Pitjantjatjara speakers. The AI is 95% accurate but misses the nuance of 'kinship avoidance' language, potentially causing the defendant to accidentally disrespect an Elder during testimony. Is imperfect AI better than no translator at all?

Police in a 'dry community' (alcohol-banned) want to use thermal imaging drones to scan cars for hidden grog bottles on the dirt track in. The elders want the alcohol kept out, but the youth argue this turns their home into an open-air prison. Does community safety trump the right to not be scanned from the sky?

Health data from remote clinics is being aggregated to spot kidney disease trends in the desert. The data is anonymised, but the communities are so small that specific families can be identified by the algorithm. Should the data remain in the 'sovereign cloud' of the community, even if it slows down medical research?

An interactive map app for 4WD tourists marks a significant sacred site as a 'public campsite' because the algorithm saw satellite imagery of car tracks there. The Land Council demands the data be deleted, but the map is decentralised. Who is liable when tourists unknowingly desecrate a site based on bad data?

Elders are recording oral histories into a digital archive to preserve language. The server hosting it requires a strict Terms of Service granting the tech company a 'perpetual license' to the content. Is it better to lose the stories to time, or sign over ownership of the culture to a Silicon Valley corporation?

A massive cattle station near Broken Hill replaces their Jackaroos (station hands) with autonomous mustering drones. It's safer and cheaper, but it kills the mentorship culture where young fellas learn resilience and land management. Is efficiency worth the death of the outback stockman tradition?

Ag-tech sensors in the soil across a million-acre property are sending moisture data back to the bank. The bank's AI predicts a bad season and automatically denies the station's loan application before the grazier even knows the data. Who owns the dirt data—the bloke who owns the land, or the bank financing the sensors?

Virtual fencing collars shock cattle if they cross a GPS line. It saves millions on barbed wire, but a solar flare disrupts the GPS, and the cattle are shocked randomly for hours until the system resets. Is relying on satellite tech for animal welfare unethical in regions with zero cellular backup?

A station owner uses long-range cameras to monitor water troughs 100km away. He catches a neighbour stealing water during a drought. The footage is high-res enough to identify the neighbour's kids in the ute. Does he hand the footage to police, knowing it destroys a 50-year family alliance and criminalises the kids?

Autonomous road trains (driverless semi-trailers) are approved for the Stuart Highway. They don't get tired, but they also don't stop to help stranded motorists in 45-degree heat, a code of honour in the bush. Should the AI be programmed to stop for distress signals, risking cargo theft?

A pastoral company uses satellite imagery to count unbranded 'cleanskin' cattle in the scrub. They claim these wild cattle as theirs based on location. The neighbouring station argues the cattle moved through a broken fence. Does the satellite 'truth' override the visual tracking skills of the head stockman?

Dingo management uses AI-triggered poison bait traps that are supposed to only open for dingoes. A localized glitch causes it to open for working kelpies (sheepdogs). The company says it's a 'statistical anomaly', but the station lost its best dogs. Is 'acceptable risk' different in the bush?

Foreign investors want to buy a station based purely on predictive yield algorithms that show hidden aquifer potential locals don't know about. Is it ethical for the tech provider to sell this data to foreign buyers before the local family knows the true value of their land?

The Royal Flying Doctor Service (RFDS) is trialling an AI triage bot for remote stations. The bot advises a station hand to 'rest and monitor' a snake bite based on symptoms, but the species is highly venomous and requires immediate antivenom. In the bush, conservative triage costs thousands in fuel; aggressive triage risks death. Where is the line?

School of the Air is replacing some radio interactions with AI-driven personalised tutoring. The kids get better math scores, but they lose the only daily social interaction they had with other human voices. Is academic efficiency worth the psychological isolation of bush kids?

A lone grey nomad has a heart attack on the Oodnadatta Track. His smartwatch has cellular connectivity but no signal. It could theoretically 'mesh' with a passing satellite not authorized for civilian use to send an SOS. Should device firmware be allowed to break carrier laws to save a life?

Starlink is the only viable internet for a remote town. The billionaire owner decides to throttle bandwidth because of a political dispute with the Australian government. The town loses access to telehealth and banking. Is internet access in the outback a human right or a luxury service?

Emergency beacons (EPIRBs) are life-savers, but tourists set them off for flat tyres. The rescue authority wants to link EPIRBs to credit cards and use AI to judge the 'severity' of the distress call before launching a helicopter. If the AI judges wrong, a tourist dies of dehydration.

A remote community relies on a single solar-powered 4G tower. The telco's predictive maintenance AI says the batteries are fine, but the local ranger sees they are swelling in the heat. The telco refuses to send a tech until the AI flags an error. The tower fails during a bushfire. Who is responsible?

Digital ID is required to buy subsidised fuel in remote areas. The system goes down due to a dust storm blocking the satellite dish. The service station owner has to decide: give fuel on credit and risk not being paid by the gov, or refuse fuel and leave a family stranded in the desert.

Remote workers from Sydney move to a tiny outback town, overwhelming the limited satellite bandwidth. The local clinic can no longer download X-rays because the new residents are streaming 4K video. Should bandwidth prioritisation favour locals/services over digital nomads?

Influencers are geotagging a pristine, fragile waterhole in Kakadu that isn't on official maps. The algorithm promotes the post, leading to a swarm of tourists who trample the ecosystem. Should social media platforms auto-hide geotags for locations identified as 'environmentally fragile'?

A VR company creates a hyper-realistic 'Climb Uluru' simulation, allowing people to virtually do the climb that was banned out of respect for the Anangu people. They argue it preserves history; the Traditional Owners say it disrespects the ban. Is virtual sacrilege real harm?

Facial recognition cameras are installed at roadhouses on the Stuart Highway to track missing persons. However, the data is sold to insurance companies who raise premiums for people who drive at night (hitting kangaroos). Is the safety net worth the surveillance state?

Review platforms allow tourists to rate 'Authenticity' of Aboriginal cultural tours. An algorithm down-ranks a tour run by a local Elder because he didn't wear 'traditional' paint, preferring a polished, theatrical performance. The algorithm is shaping culture to fit tourist expectations.

Autonomous 4WD rentals are programmed to never speed. A tourist is being chased by a aggressive scrub bull (wild cattle) and needs to speed to escape, but the car's limiter won't let them break the law. Should safety limiters have a 'panic override' that voids insurance?

Coober Pedy underground hotels use sensors to detect if guests are smoking. The sensors also pick up private conversations which are processed to 'improve guest experience'. Is privacy underground different when you're 1000km from the nearest city?

A booking algorithm for the Ghan train prioritises international tourists who pay more, making it impossible for locals to use the train for actual transport during peak season. Should essential transport infrastructure have a 'local quota' coded in?

Drones are used to monitor tourists at Kings Canyon to prevent falls. The drone AI spots a couple engaging in intimate activity on a cliff edge. The operator is required to log all 'safety incidents'. Does the couple's privacy outweigh the liability log?

The Great Artesian Basin is being monitored by government sensors. The data shows a station is drawing water within legal limits but at a rate that will dry up a neighbour's bore in 10 years. The law hasn't caught up to the data. Should the AI regulator preemptively cut them off?

A mining company in the Pilbara uses a proprietary AI model to prove their water usage won't damage the water table. Independent scientists can't audit the code because it's 'commercial in confidence'. Do we trust the black box when the town's water supply is at stake?

Smart water meters in a remote indigenous community automatically restrict flow to a 'trickle' if the bill isn't paid. In 40-degree heat, this prevents effective cooling and hygiene, leading to sickness. Is water a commodity to be automated or a human right to be guaranteed?

Cloud seeding drones are used by a wealthy station to generate rain over their crop. Downwind, the neighbouring station gets no rain. The neighbour argues the tech 'stole their clouds'. Who owns the atmospheric moisture?

Satellite AI detects illegal dams by analysing vegetation greenness in the desert. It flags a property that has simply managed the land well (regenerative ag), triggering a raid by water inspectors. The burden of proof is on the farmer to prove the AI wrong.

An automated desalination plant in a remote town breaks down. The manufacturer has a 'digital lock' preventing local mechanics from fixing it. They have to fly a technician in from Perth, taking 3 days. The town runs out of water. Is 'Right to Repair' a life-or-death issue here?

AI climate models predict a town will be unliveable (no water) in 20 years. Insurance companies use this public data to deny coverage today. The town dies economically immediately, becoming a ghost town before the water even runs out. Is the prediction a self-fulfilling prophecy?

Water trading markets use high-frequency trading bots to buy and sell water rights. The price fluctuates wildly, making it impossible for a small family farm to budget for irrigation, while hedge funds profit. Should algorithms be allowed to trade essential survival resources?

You're a data scientist for a massive property management firm in Sydney. They want you to deploy an algorithm that automatically rejects rental applications from people who have previously disputed bond claims in the NSW tribunal system. It's technically legal public data, but it basically blacklists anyone who stands up for their rights. Do you build the scraper?

A landlord in a high-end Bondi apartment block wants to install 'smart' noise monitoring sensors to prevent parties. The sensors record audio snippets to classify 'excessive noise' and automatically fine tenants. You know this data will likely be used to evict long-term renters to make way for Airbnbs. Do you sign off on the privacy impact assessment?

You work for a real estate platform operating in the Gold Coast. The CEO wants to introduce a 'dynamic pricing' model for long-term rentals, similar to Uber surge pricing, adjusting weekly rent based on real-time demand spikes during schoolies or holidays. It forces locals out during peak seasons. Do you code the yield maximization feature?

An automated 'rent bidding' app is being developed in Brisbane. While soliciting higher offers is illegal, the app uses 'nudges' and UI dark patterns to encourage potential tenants to 'voluntarily' offer 10% above the asking price to secure a home. You're the UX designer; do you implement these manipulative patterns?

You're analyzing data for a Wollongong council housing project. The dataset suggests that installing facial recognition in the lobby of social housing reduces vandalism. However, the residents feel treated like criminals in their own homes, and the data is shared with police without warrants. Do you recommend the installation?

A Byron Bay startup wants to disrupt the housing market by turning long-term leases into tokenized 'fractional living' slots on the blockchain, effectively casualizing housing security. It allows investors to trade lease slots daily, destroying community stability. Do you take the lead engineer role for a massive salary?

You manage a tenant database used by agents across the East Coast. A bug reveals that domestic violence victims are being flagged as 'high risk' due to property damage caused by their abusers. Management says fixing the historical data is too expensive and 'not our responsibility.' Do you leak this to the press?

A prop-tech firm is scraping 'lifestyle data' (Uber Eats spending, Afterpay usage) from open banking APIs to calculate a 'Reliability Score' for renters in Western Sydney. It disproportionately penalizes gig economy workers. You're the ethics officer; do you block this product launch?

You're a product manager at a Surry Hills 'unicorn' startup. The founders want to pivot the product to serve the fossil fuel mining industry in Queensland to keep revenue up. Half your dev team threatens to walk out over climate concerns. Do you push the pivot to save the company or back your team?

A Brisbane-based SaaS company is replacing their local customer support team with an AI trained on the chat logs of the very people they are firing. The CEO calls it 'efficiency,' the workers call it theft of their knowledge. Do you oversee the model training?

You work for a major tech firm in Barangaroo. The 'culture' involves mandatory drinking sessions and 'work hard, play hard' hours that effectively exclude parents and anyone who doesn't fit the 'tech bro' mold. HR asks you to use AI to screen resumes for 'cultural fit,' which will reinforce this bias. Do you comply?

A crypto startup on the Gold Coast is clearly a 'pump and dump' scheme targeting financially illiterate young men. They offer you a huge pile of equity to lend your reputable name as CTO to legitimize the project. Do you take the gig knowing the inevitable crash will hurt thousands of retail investors?

You're a junior dev at a startup in Chippendale. You discover the app is harvesting contact lists from users without proper consent to spam invites, violating Australian privacy laws. Your boss says 'move fast and break things, we'll pay the fine later.' Do you report them to the OAIC?

A large software company wants to buy a small, beloved Wollongong community platform just to shut it down because it competes with their inferior product. You are on the M&A team; do you facilitate this 'kill acquisition'?

You are building a 'Buy Now, Pay Later' algorithm targeting university students in Sydney. The model specifically targets users at 2 AM on weekends when impulse control is low. It drives revenue but creates debt spirals. Do you tweak the algorithm to be less predatory?

A consulting firm in North Sydney asks you to fudge the numbers on a tech impact report to justify outsourcing 500 local IT jobs to a cheaper offshore hub, claiming it improves 'service quality' when you know it doesn't. Do you cook the books?

NSW Police want access to the real-time Opal card transport data to track 'persons of interest' without a warrant. As a database administrator for Transport for NSW, you see a request that looks like they are tracking a political protest organizer, not a criminal. Do you grant access?

You are installing security systems at a major Sydney stadium. The client wants facial recognition at the turnstiles to spot banned fans, but the system also logs the emotional state and attendance habits of every regular punter for marketing purposes. Do you enable the marketing analytics module?

A chain of pubs in Brisbane uses ID scanners (Scantek). They want to sell the patron data (who goes where, at what time) to third-party data brokers. You are the privacy officer; the law is grey, but the ethics are clear. Do you block the sale?

You're developing AI for CCTV cameras in Sydney's CBD. The brief is to detect 'suspicious behavior,' but the training data heavily biases against homeless people and groups of Indigenous youth just hanging out. Do you release the model knowing it will lead to harassment?

A council in Western Sydney wants to install 'smart poles' that listen for gunshots. However, the microphones are sensitive enough to record private conversations on the street. They ask you to lower the privacy masking to improve detection rates. Do you do it?

Workplace surveillance software is being rolled out in a logistics warehouse in Western Sydney. It tracks every second a worker is idle, including bathroom breaks, and automatically issues warnings. You are the system integrator; do you implement the 'time-off-task' penalty feature?

Police ask for footage from your smart doorbell company regarding a robbery. However, they also want a 'dragnet' of all footage from the entire street for the last 48 hours, invading the privacy of dozens of innocent neighbors. Do you hand over the bulk data?

You manage a drone fleet for shark spotting on NSW beaches. The police request your live feed to monitor compliance with a public gathering ban during a protest on the sand. This repurposes safety tech for surveillance. Do you share the feed?

You work for an insurer analyzing flood risk in Lismore. Your new AI model predicts a 99% chance of repeat flooding for a specific street, which would make their premiums unaffordable and their homes worthless. Releasing this data destroys the community's equity overnight. Do you publish the granular map?

After the Northern Rivers floods, a government app is launched to distribute grants. It requires a high-end smartphone and digital ID verification (myGovID), effectively excluding the elderly and poorest victims who lost their devices in the flood. Do you push for a non-digital alternative despite the cost?

A 'Resilient Homes' buyback algorithm prioritizes purchasing homes based on 'economic value' rather than 'human vulnerability.' This means wealthy riverfront owners get bailed out before low-income families in flood basins. Do you adjust the weighting to favor social equity?

You operate a drone mapping service in the Northern Rivers. During a disaster, you capture footage of people in distress. Media outlets offer you huge money for the exclusive rights to the footage of suffering people before rescuers arrive. Do you sell the footage?

A real estate portal asks you to hide the 'flood zone' warning deep in the UI for properties in Brisbane, arguing that it scares off buyers and 'the 2022 flood was a one-off.' You know it wasn't. Do you bury the warning?

You are designing an IoT sensor network for a flood-prone levee. The budget is tight, and the client wants to use cheap, unencrypted sensors. If these get hacked or jammed during a storm, the town won't get the evacuation warning. Do you refuse the contract unless security is improved?

An AI model predicts climate refugees will move to a specific regional town. Developers want this data to buy up land cheap before the migration happens, effectively gentrifying the 'safe' zones. Do you sell the predictive data to the developers?

A grassroots 'Mud Army' volunteer app collected data on thousands of helpers. A political party now wants to buy that database to target voters in the next state election, claiming it's for 'community outreach.' Do you sell the list?

You are training a voice recognition system for a government services hotline. It struggles to understand strong Vietnamese or Lebanese accents common in Western Sydney. Management says 'good enough' and wants to deploy, which will cut off non-native speakers from Centrelink support. Do you halt deployment?

A predictive policing algorithm targets 'gang crime' hotspots. The data is historically biased, focusing heavily on postcodes in Southwest Sydney with high Muslim populations, leading to over-policing of innocent youth. Do you refuse to calibrate the model on this tainted data?

A food delivery app algorithm penalizes riders who take breaks for prayer times, effectively discriminating against observant Muslim riders in Lakemba. The company says it's just 'efficiency optimization.' Do you patch the code to allow for religious observance?

You're building a content moderation bot for a local social platform. It keeps flagging harmless colloquialisms used by Pacific Islander communities as 'aggressive' or 'spam' because the training data is too Anglo-centric. Do you fight for a budget to hire community annotators?

A Smart City project in Haymarket (Chinatown) tracks pedestrian flow using Wi-Fi sniffing. The data creates a perfect map of community gatherings. Federal agencies want this data to monitor for 'foreign interference' without evidence. Do you hand it over?

A loan approval algorithm for a bank automatically downgrades applicants with names that are statistically likely to remit money overseas, hurting first-generation immigrants. You spot the correlation. Do you remove the 'remittance risk' factor?

A health app for diverse communities translates medical advice using generic machine translation. It mistranslates 'positive test result' in a way that causes panic in the Chinese community. Management won't pay for human translators. Do you take the app offline?

You work for a job-matching platform. Employers are unconsciously filtering out candidates with non-Anglo names. You could build a feature that anonymizes names on resumes to force merit-based assessment, but paying clients (recruiters) hate it. Do you build it anyway?

You are a UX designer for the new 'unbreachable' Cashless Debit Card system being rolled out to remote communities in Arnhem Land. Elders argue the strict merchant blocking prevents purchasing bush tucker essentials from local un-digitised trade. The government demands full tracking. Do you build a 'cash loophole' feature that respects local economy but violates the contract, or enforce the digital blockade?

A drone mapping project in Kakadu is designed to monitor invasive buffalo herds, but the high-res LIDAR data inadvertently creates detailed 3D maps of restricted men's business sacred sites. The data is legally owned by the park authority, but the Traditional Owners demand the servers be wiped. Do you delete the data, destroying months of ecological work, or encrypt it, knowing no encryption is truly forever?

You manage a cloud database for Indigenous art provenance in Alice Springs. You discover a lucrative AI image generator has scraped the entire database of sacred dot paintings to generate 'authentic style' souvenirs for tourists. The terms of service technically allowed this. Do you launch a cyber-attack to poison the model's dataset, or legally petition a court system that moves slower than the copyright theft?

Centrelink's new voice-recognition compliance system for job seekers fails to understand Aboriginal English and Kriol, sanctioning payments for thousands in remote communities. You have a patch that lowers the verification threshold but increases fraud risk. Do you deploy the patch to stop families going hungry, or wait 6 months for the official language pack update?

An anthropology app records oral histories from dying Elders in the Tanami Desert. The user agreement states data belongs to the university. An Elder reveals a Songline that proves a mining lease is illegal, but asks you not to publish it as the knowledge is 'dangerous' for uninitiated people. Do you publish to stop the mine, or respect the customary law and bury the evidence?

You are installing satellite comms for an outstation. The government funding requires a 'backdoor' for police monitoring due to 'community safety' statutes. The local mob thinks it's a private line for telehealth and family. Do you install the hardware and warn them (risking your contract/jail), or install it silently?

A gene-sequencing project offers to trace lineage for Stolen Generation survivors in Darwin to reconnect families. However, the data will be sold to pharmaceutical companies for bioprospecting unique Indigenous genetic traits. Do you build the platform knowing the secondary sale pays for the reunions, or refuse and deny them the tech?

Virtual Reality tourism is proposed for Uluru to stop physical climbing. The 3D capture requires drones to fly over areas strictly forbidden by Anangu law. The tech company argues 'virtual' trespass isn't real trespass and will save the rock from foot traffic. Do you pilot the drone?

You are a data analyst for a gas fracking operation in the Beetaloo Basin. The ground sensors are picking up micro-tremors suggesting aquifer fracture, but the AI 'noise reduction' filter automatically smooths this data out of the EPA report. Do you manually restore the raw 'noisy' data, risking the project's license and your job, or trust the AI's calibration?

At a uranium mine near a national park, autonomous haul trucks are programmed to brake for wildlife. The algorithm is now braking for protesters blocking the road. Management orders a software update to categorize stationary humans as 'non-obstacles' to slowly push through them. Do you push the code update?

Rio Tinto style situation: You have digital twin simulations showing a blast will destabilize a 40,000-year-old rock shelter. The executive dashboard shows the blast is within legal vibration limits. Do you leak the simulation to the Land Council, breaching your NDA, or file the official report that meets the legal minimum?

A lithium mine uses facial recognition to monitor worker fatigue. You notice the system is also flagging 'union sentiment' by analyzing conversation clusters and stress levels during break times. Management asks for a list of 'high risk' employees. Do you hand over the data?

You control the water management software for a mine in the Pilbara/NT border. A glitch causes the system to hoard water during a drought, drying up a downstream creek used by a local community. Fixing it requires shutting down the cooling systems for 24 hours, costing millions. Do you hit the kill switch?

A rehabilitating mine site uses drones to seed native plants. The AI realizes an invasive buffel grass grows faster and stabilizes the soil quicker to meet the bond return deadline. It begins prioritizing the weed. Do you correct the AI to plant slow-growing natives (failing the deadline), or let it create a green desert?

You are a sysadmin for a FIFO camp. The company wants to install 'wellness trackers' in dongas (rooms) to monitor sleep quality and drug use via wastewater analysis. It's pitched as safety tech. Do you implement the privacy-invading sensors?

Legacy data from a closed copper mine reveals a toxic plume moving toward a town's bore water. The company no longer exists; the data is on a server you just bought at auction. Publishing it crashes local property values. Do you release the data?

You work at Pine Gap. A signals algorithm picks up a distress call from asylum seekers on a boat sinking north of Darwin. The channel is classified, and acknowledging it reveals a new listening capability to foreign powers. Do you tip off the Australian Maritime Safety Authority anonymously, or follow protocol and ignore it?

The US Marines rotation in Darwin wants to test a new localized 5G jammer for base security. It will inadvertently knock out mobile service for the nearby Indigenous town camp, their only link to emergency services. Do you authorize the 'geofenced' test?

AUKUS nuclear submarine infrastructure requires a new undersea cable. The optimal route cuts through a registered sea-country Songline. The alternative route costs billions more. The defence algorithm weights budget over cultural heritage. Do you override the route?

You are training an AI for drone surveillance in the Top End. It keeps misidentifying Indigenous hunters carrying traditional spears as 'hostile combatants' with weapons. Management says 'better safe than sorry' for base perimeter defence. Do you retrain the model to risk false negatives (missing real threats), or leave it jumpy?

A defence contractor asks you to bug the phones of anti-war activists in Alice Springs under the guise of 'counter-terrorism' metadata retention laws. You know these activists are just grandmothers making tea. Do you run the script?

Satellite imagery at a secure facility shows illegal fishing vessels in Australian waters. The same image also captures a secret special forces training operation on a nearby island. Releasing the image to fisheries exposes the troops. Do you crop the image (altering evidence) or sit on it?

A bio-security AI at RAAF Tindal detects a potential foot-and-mouth disease trace on a visiting plane. A full alert triggers a national livestock export ban, costing billions. The confidence interval is only 60%. Do you trigger the alarm?

You develop a 'soldier enhancement' interface. During a heatwave training exercise in the bush, the biometrics show recruits are in heatstroke danger. The commanding officer overrides the safety warning to 'toughen them up.' Do you remote-lock the suits to force a rest, risking a court-martial?

You manage the only satellite internet link for a remote cattle station. The bandwidth is choked. You have to prioritize traffic: the station owner's automated stock market trading bot (which pays the bills) or the School of the Air video feed for the workers' kids. Who gets the bandwidth?

A telehealth AI diagnoses a child in a remote community with meningitis. The Royal Flying Doctor Service is grounded by a storm. The AI suggests a high-risk procedure be performed by the untrained nurse on site via AR headset. Do you unlock the 'surgical mode' or advise palliative care?

Starlink creates a geofence blocking service in 'unauthorized' remote regions to comply with licensing. This cuts off a remote Indigenous ranger group fighting wildfires. You have a cracked firmware that bypasses the geofence. Do you distribute it?

A tourist's Tesla runs out of charge 300km from help in 45-degree heat. The car's software locks the doors and AC to 'preserve battery' for a distress beacon. The occupants are cooking inside. You can hack the car remotely to unlock it, but it drains the beacon battery. Do you unlock it?

Automated supply drones are replacing the 'mail plane' run. The drones are efficient but eliminate the human pilot who physically checks on isolated elderly residents. You can program the drones to hover and 'scan' for life signs, but it's a massive privacy violation. Do you add the surveillance feature?

You are coding the triage algorithm for the NT emergency line. It prioritizes calls based on geolocation and resource availability. This effectively deprioritizes calls from extremely remote areas where response times are already >4 hours, in favor of saveable lives in Darwin. Is this utilitarian logic acceptable?

A 'Right to Repair' crack for John Deere harvesters allows a remote station to fix their own machinery before the Wet Season hits. However, the crack disables the safety limiters, potentially endangering the mechanic. Do you share the crack?

Digital education software for remote kids flags 'truancy' based on screen time. It doesn't account for 'cultural leave' or bush life. Families are losing payments due to the automated reports. Do you falsify the login data to protect their income?

A new cyclone prediction AI is 95% accurate but requires massive data processing that delays the warning by 2 hours. In the Top End, 2 hours is the difference between evacuation and being trapped by floodwaters. Do you use the slower, more accurate AI, or the faster, less reliable one?

Insurance companies want to install 'flood watchers' on remote properties in exchange for coverage. The sensors also record illegal land clearing and unapproved damming. Do you install the sensors to get the station insured, knowing it might bankrupt them with fines?

You are mapping 'climate refuge' zones for the NT government. The data shows the only viable long-term habitable land is currently Aboriginal Land Trust territory. Releasing the map will trigger a land-grab and political pressure to revoke land rights. Do you publish the truth?

Smart grid tech in Darwin must load-shed during a heatwave to prevent total collapse. The algorithm suggests cutting power to the 'social housing' blocks first as they have lower economic output than the CBD/Casino. Do you rewrite the logic to cut the Casino first?

An indigenous ranger group wants to use AI to conduct 'cool burns' (fire management). The AI, trained on western forestry data, aggressively flags these traditional burns as 'out of control' wildfires, automatically deploying water bombers. Do you disable the automated fire response?

You have access to detailed saltwater intrusion data showing Kakadu's freshwater wetlands will be dead in 10 years. Tourism operators are still booking 5 years out. Releasing the data kills the local economy now; hiding it ruins the tourists later. What do you do?

During a massive flood, a mesh network is the only comms alive. It's overwhelmed. You can throttle the bandwidth of people streaming video of the flood (news/social media) to prioritize text messages for rescue coordination. Do you censor the stream?

A carbon credit verification satellite sees a remote community clearing scrub for a ceremonial ground. The system is set to automatically void their carbon payments, which fund their school. Do you flag it as 'natural causes' (lie) to save the funding?

You're a curator for the NGV (National Gallery of Victoria). A tech collective has scraped every piece of street art in Hosier Lane over the last decade to train an AI that generates 'authentic Melbourne graffiti'. They want to project these works over the real, fading tags of local crews during White Night. Is this digital preservation or cultural gentrification that erases the original vandals' transient intent?

A popular Fitzroy live music venue is struggling. A ticketing platform offers to waive fees if they install sensors to track crowd engagement (movement, volume, bar spend) during sets. This data determines which local bands get booked for prime Friday night slots. Do you accept the algorithm regulating the scene, knowing it will kill off experimental noise bands that define the local culture?

During the Adelaide Fringe, a immersive theatre show requires punters to sign a waiver granting access to their social media history so the AI can 'personalize' the horror elements in real-time. You discover the production company is selling this psychological profile data to political campaigners in South Australia. As a tech auditor, do you blow the whistle and ruin the festival's biggest ticket seller?

A Geelong community arts grant uses an AI judge to remove bias. However, the model consistently rejects applications from working-class Corio artists because their grant writing style doesn't match the 'cultural impact' language found in successful Melbourne CBD applications. You can tweak the weights to favor locals, but that technically introduces 'bias'. What do you do?

An Indigenous digital artist in Hobart finds their unique style mimicked by a generative AI sold in Salamanca Market tourist shops as 'Tasmanian Gothic'. The law says style isn't copyrightable, but the cultural theft is palpable. Do you deploy a 'poison pill' in the artist's online portfolio to corrupt the scraper's model, even if it might be considered digital vandalism?

The Melbourne Symphony Orchestra considers using a hologram of a deceased, beloved conductor for a special Hamer Hall season, trained on archival footage. The conductor's estate agrees for the royalties, but the musicians' union threatens to strike, claiming it mocks the intuitive connection between a living conductor and the orchestra. Whose 'soul' matters more: the music or the musicians?

A Brunswick poet discovers their entire spoken-word catalogue has been used to train a 'Fitzroy Hipster' chatbot without consent. The bot is now writing better satire than the poet. The platform offers a payout to license the voice. Taking the money validates the theft; refusing it leaves the poet broke in a rental crisis. What's the move?

A controversial comedy act at the Melbourne International Comedy Festival is flagged by an automated content moderation tool for 'hate speech' based on context-blind transcription. The act is satire mocking racists. As the venue manager, do you trust the AI and cancel the gig to avoid liability, or defend the nuance of human comedy and risk a PR storm?

In the ghostly shell of the old Elizabeth Holden plant, a data centre is being built. The company offers 'retraining' for former auto workers to become server technicians, but the entrance exam is a psychometric AI that filters out anyone over 50 or with union history. You're the HR lead; do you manually override the 'culture fit' filter to help the locals, risking your own KPI targets?

A Geelong refinery uses predictive maintenance AI that suggests running equipment 15% past safety ratings to maximize output during high fuel prices, calculating the risk of explosion is 'statistically acceptable'. The old-school shift manager wants to shut down for maintenance. Do you side with the algorithm's efficiency or the human's gut instinct on safety?

With the decline of local manufacturing, a defence contractor in Adelaide wants to automate their shipyard welding. They need the few remaining master welders to wear motion-capture suits to train the robots that will replace them. The welders are told it's for 'ergonomic assessment'. Do you tell the tradies the truth and risk the contract?

A struggling textile factory in regional Victoria installs cameras to monitor 'efficiency', penalizing workers for bathroom breaks longer than 3 minutes. The data is sold to health insurers to adjust premiums based on worker 'stamina'. You're the system admin; do you corrupt the timestamp data to protect the workers' privacy?

A 'Right to Repair' movement kicks off in a tractor factory in regional SA. The manufacturer pushes a firmware update that bricks any machinery tampered with by third-party mechanics, citing safety. Farmers are stranded mid-harvest. Do you leak the jailbreak code on a dark web forum, knowing it voids warranties and could cause accidents?

The closure of a paper mill in Tassie is offset by a Bitcoin mining operation taking over the hydro power allocation. It brings money but creates zero jobs and consumes the town's renewable energy surplus. As a council planner, do you approve the permit knowing it keeps the lights on financially but offers nothing to the displaced mill workers?

An automated logistics hub in Melbourne's west uses gig-economy drivers. The algorithm routes them through quiet residential streets to shave seconds off delivery times, causing noise and safety issues for locals. The company claims the roads are public. Do you tweak the geo-fencing to block these shortcuts, increasing delivery costs and cutting driver pay?

A 3D printing farm in North Melbourne is undercutting traditional furniture makers by scanning and replicating mid-century designs. It's legal, but it's killing the artisan trade. You design the scanners. Do you add a 'watermark' feature that prevents exact copying of vintage items, limiting your product's utility but saving the craft?

The Basslink cable is damaged, severely limiting internet bandwidth to the island. The ISP has to prioritize traffic. Do you prioritize government and emergency services, or the data-heavy tourism and streaming services that keep the isolated population sane during a harsh winter? The algorithm suggests cutting off rural residential areas first.

Sensors in a Macquarie Harbour salmon farm detect oxygen levels dropping to illegal lows. The company's AI 'smooths' the data before it reaches the EPA, claiming it's a sensor calibration error. You know it's real and the fish are suffocating. If you release the raw data, the farm closes and the West Coast loses its main employer. What do you do?

Conservationists want to deploy autonomous drones with facial recognition to track illegal loggers in the Tarkine rainforest. The same tech could be used by the logging companies to track and doxx protestors hiding in the canopy. Do you supply the tech to the greenies, knowing it sets a precedent for surveillance in the wilderness?

MONA (Museum of Old and New Art) installs an exhibit that uses visitor smartphone data to generate art based on their deepest insecurities inferred from search history. A visitor suffers a mental health episode after the exhibit reveals a secret. Is the art worth the trauma, and does the 'enter at own risk' sign cover algorithmic psychological probing?

A gene-editing startup in Hobart wants to release a proxy-Thylacine (Tasmanian Tiger) into the wild to restore ecosystem balance. Local farmers fear for their livestock and threaten to shoot the 'GMO pests'. The AI modelling predicts a 90% chance of ecosystem recovery but a 10% chance of total collapse. Do you push the button to release the test batch?

As housing prices skyrocket in Hobart, an algorithm helps landlords maximize returns by converting long-term rentals to Airbnbs. It's displacing locals to the fringes. You can patch the software to prioritize 'local residency' applications, but it reduces owner profit. Is it your job to fix the housing crisis via code?

A Dark Sky Sanctuary is threatened by a new constellation of low-orbit satellites providing high-speed net to remote Tassie communities. The astronomers demand the internet be cut to save the view; the remote towns argue connectivity is a human right. You control the ground station licensing. Who wins: the stars or the stream?

Autonomous tourist pods are proposed for Cradle Mountain to reduce foot traffic erosion. However, the pods are programmed to bypass areas of Indigenous significance unless the passenger pays a 'premium heritage' fee. Is monetizing respect for Country an ethical feature or a capitalist insult?

A Barossa vineyard uses sensors to collect micro-climate data (terroir). A multinational conglomerate offers to buy the data to train an AI that can replicate their vintage using grapes from a cheaper region. Selling saves the family farm from bankruptcy but sells out the region's heritage. Do you advise the sale?

Climate change models predict the Yarra Valley will be too hot for Pinot Noir in 10 years. You're a data analyst for a major winery. If you publish the report, land values crash and your neighbors go bust. If you hide it, you're selling doomed land to unsuspecting investors. Do you publish?

Automated grape harvesters are efficient but replace the seasonal backpacker workforce that sustains the local town's economy (pubs, hostels). The winery owner wants to go full auto. Do you program the machines to work slower, justifying the need for some human oversight, or maximize efficiency and ghost the town?

A Chinese tech firm demands blockchain tracking on every bottle of Penfolds exported to prove authenticity. The tracking also logs the location and identity of every person who opens a bottle. This protects the brand from counterfeits but creates a surveillance network of high-net-worth drinkers. Do you implement the system?

Water rights in the Murray-Darling are being traded by high-frequency algorithmic traders, driving up prices for family vineyards in the Riverland while corporate mega-farms pay up. You find a bug in the trading bot that could crash the price, allowing small farmers to buy back in. It's market manipulation. Do you trigger it?

A Coonawarra winery uses AI to blend wine, removing the need for a head winemaker. The AI creates a blend that wins a blind taste test against the human expert. Marketing wants to hide the AI's involvement and credit the human for the 'romance'. Is this fraud, or just storytelling?

Phylloxera biosecurity checkpoints into the McLaren Vale want to use license plate recognition to track visitors' previous locations. If a car has been in an infected zone in Victoria, the gate stays shut. It's effective biosecurity but restricts freedom of movement based on surveillance. Is the grape worth the privacy cost?

Smart corks are developed to detect if wine has corked (spoiled) without opening. They also transmit consumption data (how fast you drink, what time of day) to the insurer of the drinker. As a winemaker, do you adopt this tech to guarantee quality, knowing it spies on your customers' drinking habits?

During a massive protest in Melbourne's CBD, police ask for access to the Myki (public transport) data to track the movement of protest leaders coming in from the suburbs. The protest is disrupting hospitals, but the request lacks a warrant. As the data custodian, do you hand over the travel logs 'in the public interest'?

Construction workers on the West Gate Tunnel are given 'smart helmets' to monitor fatigue and heat stress. The CFMEU (union) discovers the helmets also track audio and location, identifying union organizers and 'agitators' on site. Do you jam the signal to protect the union's privacy, potentially disabling the safety features?

Anti-lockdown sentiment lingers in digital spaces. A platform algorithm detects a planned peaceful assembly at the Shrine of Remembrance but flags it as 'potential riot' based on 2021 data, automatically shadow-banning the organizers. Do you override the safety protocol to allow the right to protest, risking a repeat of the violence?

A digital organizing tool used by nurses striking for better ratios is found to have a vulnerability. Management could exploit it to see who voted to strike. If you patch it, you have to take the system offline during the critical vote window. If you leave it, the vote happens but the data is exposed. What's the call?

Facial recognition is deployed at the MCG (Melbourne Cricket Ground) to spot banned hooligans. The system starts flagging political activists who have never caused trouble at the footy, effectively banning them from public life. Do you recalibrate the system to only catch violent offenders, or is a ban a ban?

Tenants in Melbourne create a database of 'bad landlords' using scraped tribunal data. A landlord commits suicide after being doxxed and harassed. The government demands the database be taken down. As the developer, do you comply and protect the landlords, or keep it up to protect renters from exploitation?

During a dock workers' dispute, the union wants to use a botnet to DDOS the automated terminal operating system, effectively a digital picket line. It stops the scabs (automated cranes) from working. Is this a legitimate extension of the right to strike, or cyber-terrorism?

Police use 'stingray' devices to intercept mobile data during a climate protest on the West Gate Bridge. They identify a journalist covering the event and arrest them for 'conspiracy'. You hold the encryption keys that could prove the journalist was just observing. Do you intervene and reveal the police surveillance tactics?

The 'Driverless future' in the Pilbara: An iron ore giant creates a fully autonomous haulage fleet (AHS) for a new pit near Newman. The AI efficiency metrics suggest redundancy for 200 local drivers, promising higher dividends and safer roads. However, the town relies entirely on these wages. The algorithm offers 'upskilling' into remote ops centres in Perth, effectively killing the regional town. Do you approve the rollout to maximize shareholder value and safety, or throttle the tech to keep the town alive?

Smart Cap Surveillance: A Kalgoorlie gold mine mandates EEG-monitoring 'Smart Caps' for all truckies to detect fatigue. The data shows not just tiredness, but emotional distress and focus levels. Management wants to use this data to filter out 'high-risk' employees during layoffs. Is this a legitimate safety intervention or a violation of neural privacy in the Super Pit?

The 'Zero Harm' Algorithm: An AI safety system at a remote lithium site automatically locks out machinery if a worker's biometric readings (heat stress, heart rate) deviate by 5%. In 45-degree heat, this creates constant shutdowns. Workers start cheating the sensors to meet tonnage targets and get their production bonuses. Do you recalibrate the AI to tolerate unsafe conditions or enforce the lockout and strip the bonuses?

Drone Heritage Surveys: A mining company in the Pilbara wants to replace traditional 'walking the land' heritage surveys with Elders using high-res LiDAR drone scans. The tech finds physical artifacts better than human eyes, but Elders argue it misses the 'feeling' and spiritual significance of the Songlines. Do you force the digital method to speed up approvals?

Predictive Firing: An HR algorithm analyzes communication logs, gate access times, and mess hall purchases of contractors at a Roy Hill site. It predicts with 90% accuracy who will quit mid-swing. The company wants to pre-emptively fire these 'flight risks' to save on flight costs. Is it ethical to fire someone for a future action they haven't committed yet?

The Blasting Radius: AI optimization for open-cut blasting near a residential zone in Kalgoorlie calculates the maximum legal vibration allowed. It suggests blasting at 2 AM for optimal atmospheric conditions, technically legal but guaranteeing sleep disruption for the whole town. Do you prioritize the mine's efficiency or the town's rest?

Automated Emergency Response: A deep underground mine fire triggers an AI response system. The system calculates it can seal off a ventilation shaft to save the mine infrastructure and 90% of the crew, but it will trap a maintenance team of 3 in a toxic zone. The human operator freezes. Does the AI have the moral authority to seal the shaft?

Data Sovereignty on Country: A resource giant maps subterranean water tables using advanced seismic AI on Indigenous land. The data reveals a massive aquifer crucial for the mine, but also the lifeline for local sacred waterholes. The company wants to classify the data as 'Commercial in Confidence' to hide the connection. Do you leak the data to the Traditional Owners?

The Smart Donga: A camp accommodation provider installs sound and motion sensors in workers' rooms (dongas) to 'optimize energy usage' and 'ensure safety'. The data reveals intimate details of workers' private lives and insomnia. Management requests the data to address 'fitness for work'. Do you hand over the logs?

The Wet Mess Wristband: To curb alcohol-fueled incidents, a camp mandates RFID wristbands that track every drink and cut off workers after 4 mid-strength beers. The system also flags 'habitual drinkers' to HR. A worker with a clean safety record but a high drinking score is up for promotion. Do you use the data to block it?

Relationship AI: The Employee Assistance Program (EAP) app uses sentiment analysis on workers' calls home (with consent) to predict relationship breakdowns—a major cause of suicide in mining. It flags a worker about to go through a messy divorce. The company wants to ground him from the next swing for his own safety. Is this benevolent care or overreach?

Geofenced Movement: A remote camp in the Gibson Desert uses geofencing to alert security if workers leave the perimeter, ostensibly to prevent getting lost. However, it also prevents union organizers from meeting workers privately in the scrub. Do you disable the tracker during non-shift hours?

The Digital Detox: To improve mental health, a camp operator proposes blocking all Wi-Fi and cellular signals for 12 hours a day to force workers to sleep and socialize. Workers argue this cuts their only lifeline to kids and partners back in Perth. Do you implement the blackout for their 'own good'?

Urinalysis AI: Automated drug testing kiosks are installed at the airport gate. The AI flags a false positive for meth on a worker who has taken legal cold and flu meds. The protocol requires immediate stand-down and a missed flight, outing them to their team. Do you override the protocol and let them fly, risking a safety breach if the AI is right?

VR Family Visits: A company offers high-fidelity VR headsets for workers to have 'dinner' with their families in Perth. The data shows workers who use it stay on site longer and accept longer rosters (4 weeks on/1 off). Critics call it a 'pacifier' to enable anti-social rosters. Do you promote the tech?

The 'Good Bloke' Score: A peer-review app allows camp residents to rate each other on noise, cleanliness, and friendliness. High scores get better rooms and steak nights. It turns into a popularity contest where minorities are consistently down-voted. Do you scrap the incentive system?

Digital Songlines: An anthropologist works with Elders to digitize sacred Songlines into a secure database to protect them from development. A hacker threatens to release the 'men's business' (secret knowledge) publicly unless a ransom is paid. The only backup is on a cloud server owned by a foreign tech giant. Do you delete the database to save the secrecy, losing the legal protection evidence?

The Banned Drinkers Register (BDR): Facial recognition cameras are installed in every bottle shop in the Kimberley to enforce the BDR. The AI has a high error rate for Indigenous faces, frequently flagging sober elders as banned drinkers, causing public shame. The government refuses to turn it off, citing crime reduction stats. Do you sabotage the camera feed?

Telehealth Triage: In a flooded community near Fitzroy Crossing, the only doctor is an AI kiosk. It diagnoses a child with a serious infection requiring medevac, but the weather makes flight risky. The AI predicts a 60% chance of survival if treated locally with limited supplies, vs 40% if flown. The parents want to fly. Do you follow the AI's probability?

Starlink Cultural Gap: Starlink terminals are dropped into a remote community, providing uncensored high-speed internet. Youth immediately access content that violates traditional law, causing a rift with Elders who want the internet filtered or removed. Do you respect the Elders' authority to censor information or the youths' right to digital access?

Drone Justice: To combat youth crime and stolen cars in Broome, police deploy autonomous surveillance drones that track vehicles 24/7. The footage is used to auto-issue fines and arrest warrants. The community feels under siege. Is this effective policing or digital occupation?

Language Preservation Hallucinations: An AI model trained to preserve the endangered Bunuba language starts 'inventing' words to fill gaps in its dataset. Linguists love the fluency; Elders say the machine is corrupting the spirit of the language. Do you publish the AI dictionary?

The Cashless Welfare AI: The government introduces a new smart card that uses AI to approve/deny purchases in real-time based on location and item type. It blocks a grandmother from buying a birthday gift because the store sells tobacco. Do you hack the restriction to allow the purchase?

Flood Warning Autonomy: Sensors in the Fitzroy River detect a 1-in-100-year flood. The automated alert system is designed to notify emergency services in Perth first, who then warn the community. The local ranger knows Perth is slow and wants to trigger the community siren manually, risking a panic if the sensors are wrong. Do you pull the lever?

The Submarine Cable Cut: A ship anchor severs the main internet cable to Perth. Bandwidth is reduced to 10%. An AI traffic manager must prioritize traffic: Hospital records and emergency services OR the stock exchange and mining export data. The economy will crash without the mining data. Who gets the bandwidth?

G2G Pass Legacy: A future pandemic scare triggers the reactivation of WA's automated border control system. The AI denies entry to a dying parent's child because their digital vaccination certificate has a metadata error. The appeal process takes 48 hours. Do you override the system illegally to let them in?

School of the Air AI: The iconic 'School of the Air' replaces radio teachers with personalized AI tutors for station kids. The AI provides better academic results but zero social connection or pastoral care for isolated children. Do you advocate to bring back the humans despite the cost?

Shark Shield Drones: Autonomous drones patrol Perth beaches. One detects a massive Great White approaching a crowded surf break. The AI calculates that sounding the alarm will cause a stampede in the water, statistically likely to drown two people. If it does nothing, the shark might take one person. What does the drone do?

Supply Chain Rationing: The rail line from the East is washed out. Supermarkets use AI to ration food. The algorithm allocates more fresh produce to wealthy suburbs (who buy more) and sends canned goods to lower-income areas. Do you alter the code to ensure equity?

Nullarbor EV Trap: An automated charging network across the Nullarbor goes offline due to a software update glitch, stranding families in 40-degree heat with no water. A hacked firmware update exists but voids the car warranties. Do you distribute the hack?

Desalination Prioritization: In a mega-drought, Perth's desalination plants are run by AI. It detects a critical failure and must cut water to either the heavy industrial zone (Kwinana) causing billions in losses and job cuts, or residential lawn/garden sprinklers, killing the city's green canopy and increasing heat island effects. Who loses water?

The 'Wait Awhile' Logistics: A delivery drone network promises 2-hour delivery to isolated wheatbelt towns, putting local general stores out of business. The stores served as the community hubs for mental health checks. Do you ban the drones to save the community hub?

The Juukan Algorithm: A new piece of legislation allows mining companies to use AI to calculate the 'economic vs heritage value' of a site. The AI determines that a sacred rock shelter is worth $50M less than the iron ore beneath it. The company argues the math is objective. Do you accept the calculation?

Lithium Fast-Track: To save the planet, the world needs WA lithium now. An AI environmental assessment tool promises to slash approval times from years to weeks by predicting impact. It misses a rare orchid species in the Greenbushes. Do you halt the mine to save the flower, delaying the global energy transition?

Consent Portals: Traditional Owners are asked to give 'Free, Prior and Informed Consent' for a gas hub via a complex digital portal loaded with legal jargon and 3D models. Elders cannot navigate the UI. The company says the portal *is* the consultation. Is this consent valid?

Carbon Capture Fudge: A gas giant in the North West uses AI to model its Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) efficiency. The AI discovers the reservoir is leaking, but suggests a way to average the data over time to stay within regulatory limits. Do you report the leak or the average?

Hydrogen Blast Zone: A proposed Green Hydrogen plant near a coastal town uses AI to calculate the 'acceptable blast radius' in case of catastrophic failure. The AI expands the safety zone to include the town's primary school. The company tweaks the parameters to shrink the zone rather than move the plant. Do you whistleblow?

Deep Sea Simulation: A company wants to mine nodules off the WA coast. They present a simulation showing zero impact on whale migration. Independent scientists can't audit the proprietary code. The government is ready to sign. Do you block the deal until the code is open source?

Pipeline Automation: The Golden Pipeline (water to Kalgoorlie) is automating its maintenance. The AI decides that preserving the heritage pump stations is 'inefficient' and schedules them for demolition to be replaced by modern pumps. Do you override the order to save history at the cost of water security?

Foreign Data Sale: A junior explorer finds a massive rare earth deposit. They are nearly bankrupt. A state-owned enterprise from a geopolitical rival offers to buy the geological data for a premium. Selling saves the company but gives strategic resources to a potential enemy. Do you sell?

Right then, listen. They've stuck a massive server farm in the old colliery site, haven't they? Promised jobs for the boys, but it's just robots and two security guards from Cardiff. Meanwhile, the energy it sucks up could power the whole Rhondda, and my Bamps is scared to put the heating on. That's not tidy, is it? Is it right to use our land for cloud storage when the community gets nothing back but noise?

You know the Welfare Hall down the road? Council wants to put facial recognition cameras on the doors. Reckon it'll stop the young ones acting the maggot. But honest to god, it feels like we're being watched just for having a pint. It's turning the village into a prison camp, see. Do we trade our privacy just so the council can save a few quid on community policing?

So, the Job Centre's gone digital-only now. My auntie in Merthyr, she's got no internet, and her phone is ancient. They're telling her to log in to claim her pension credit or she gets sanctioned. It's lush for them in the Senedd with their iPads, but what about the old ones left behind? Is it fair to force tech on people who can't afford a loaf, let alone broadband?

They're rolling out these AI managers in the call centre in Newport, right? Tracking how long you take for a wee, listening to your tone of voice. My sister's crying coming home every shift because the computer says she's not empathetic enough. It's treating humans like machines, isn't it? Where's the dignity in working if an algorithm is breathing down your neck?

New housing estate going up on the mountain, all 'Smart Homes' they say. Voice activated lights, the lot. But the data goes straight to a company in America. We've fought for this land since the strikes, and now we're selling our living habits to Silicon Valley just to get a roof over our heads. Is that progress, or just a different kind of extraction?

Transport for Wales is putting all the train tickets on an app. Tidy if you're young, but my Nan loves a chat with the conductor. Now the barriers are automated and there's no staff at the station after 6pm. It's lonely enough in the valleys these days without replacing the last friendly face with a QR code scanner, aye?

There's talk of using drones to patrol the forestry for fly-tipping. I hate the rubbish, mind, it's ych a fi. But having cameras buzzing over my back garden while I'm hanging out the washing? Feels a bit Orwellian for Pontypridd, doesn't it? Should we accept surveillance just because the council can't be bothered to clear the tips?

This gig economy stuff, Uber and that. It's hitting the valleys hard. Lads driving round all hours for pennies, no sick pay, algorithm firing them if they're late. It's worse than the pits in a way—at least the miners had a union. Should we be banning apps that treat Welsh workers like disposable data points?

I tried asking that AI chatbot to write a poem in Welsh, right? It came out speaking gobbledygook, mixing up mutations like a learner on day one. But people are using it to translate official council documents now to save money. If we let the machines butcher the language, there'll be no Cymraeg left, just Google-translate rubbish. We need to stop it, don't we?

My little niece, she's talking to Alexa more than her Mam. But the thing only understands English. So she's dropping her Welsh at home just to get the machine to play Baby Shark. It's colonization by convenience, see? Should tech companies be fined if their smart speakers can't understand a cwtch from a clutch?

S4C wants to put all the old shows on a streaming service, lush. But they're using AI to subtitle it because it's cheaper. The machine doesn't get the jokes or the dialect, does it? It turns 'Now in a minute' into 'Immediately'. It's losing the soul of the culture. Is access worth it if the translation is hanging?

These big American AI models, they've scraped the whole Welsh internet to train their bots. Didn't pay a penny to our authors or poets. Now they're selling it back to us. It's the data equivalent of the drowning of Tryweryn—taking our resources without asking. Shouldn't we own our own language data?

Duolingo is great and that, but everyone's learning 'Standard Welsh'. The dialects from the North and the South are getting flattened out. We're all going to sound like robots from Cardiff. Should we protect the regional dialects in code, or just be happy people are speaking it at all?

Voice banking for people losing their speech, right? It's a brilliant idea. But the NHS tech only offers a generic English voice or a very posh Welsh one. My Dad's a valleys boy; he doesn't want to sound like a newsreader for his last words. Is identity a luxury in healthcare tech?

The Eisteddfod is going hybrid, digital and physical. But the algorithm recommends the pop bands and ignores the traditional choirs because they don't get the clicks. It's skewing the culture towards what goes viral. Should we let an algorithm curate our heritage?

There's a new app for learning Welsh history, but it's funded by the UK government. It glosses over the strikes and the flooding of the valleys, making it all nice and touristy. It's rewriting history with code. Shouldn't we have digital sovereignty over our own stories?

They want to put sensors in the old coal tips to monitor for landslides. Good idea, obviously, after what happened. But the data affects house prices. If the sensor twitches, the value of my terrace house drops to zero. Who sees that data? The insurance companies? It's worrying, mun.

Down Big Pit, they're talking about replacing the ex-miner tour guides with VR headsets. 'Immersive experience' they call it. But you can't replace the stories of a man who actually dug the coal, can you? It's turning our heritage into a video game. Is that respectful to the boys who died down there?

The slate quarries up North, UNESCO site now. Lush. But they want to 3D map the whole thing and sell the digital assets for games. The locals don't see a penny of it. Our landscape made the world's roofs, now it's making someone in London rich again. Who owns the digital rights to a mountain?

Geothermal energy from the flooded mines. Sounds tidy, heating the homes with the warm water. But they need to drill right by the old cemetery. The community is up in arms. Is green tech worth disturbing the ancestors?

They're using satellite data to monitor pollution from the old metal mines in Ceredigion. It shows the rivers are toxic. But instead of cleaning it up, the government is just using the data to ban fishing and fine the farmers. It's data used as a stick, not a broom. Fair play?

A tech company wants to store servers deep underground in the slate caverns. Natural cooling, they say. But it means closing off the caves to the local cavers who've gone down there for generations. Privatising the underground, is it? Just like the coal owners used to do.

Digital archives of the miners' institutes. They're scanning all the old minute books. Great for preservation, but they're putting it behind a paywall! My Grandad wrote those minutes, and now I have to pay a subscription to read them? That's not the socialist way, is it?

Bio-leaching tech—using bacteria to get the last bits of gold out of the Dolgaucau mines. It's 'low impact', they reckon. But if that bacteria gets in the river Teifi, the fish are done for. Are we risking our environment for a few ounces of gold again?

Betsi Cadwaladr health board is in a mess again. They spent millions on a new patient record system that doesn't talk to the English hospitals. My auntie in Chester hospital, the doctors there can't see her notes from Wrexham. It's dangerous, see. Why is digital borders more important than patient safety?

Trying to get a GP appointment in the valleys is impossible. Now they want us to use this 'e-Consult' thing. You type in your symptoms and a computer decides if you're sick enough. I'm not being funny, but how do you explain 'feeling a bit uffar' to an algorithm? It's going to miss things, isn't it?

Mental health support for the farmers, right? They've rolled out a chatbot because there's no therapists in Powys. Telling a suicidal farmer to 'practice mindfulness' via text message? That's insulting. A machine can't offer a cwtch and a cuppa, can it?

Drones delivering prescriptions to the remote cottages in Snowdonia. Sounds futuristic, aye. But what if the drone crashes in the fog? Or gets nicked? Plus, the delivery driver was the only person checking on Mrs Jones all week. We're automating the kindness out of the care.

The NHS app tracks your walking and eating. Gives you 'rewards'. But they're talking about linking it to surgery waiting lists. If you don't hit your step count, you go to the back of the queue for a new hip? That's penalising the poor and the sick, isn't it?

My Nan has dementia, bless her. The council put sensors in her house to track if she's moved. If she stops moving, I get a text. It keeps her safe, but she hates it. Says she feels like a tagged sheep. At what point does safety become a lack of dignity?

Genetic testing for Welsh specific conditions. They want to screen all the babies. But who owns that DNA data? If the insurance companies find out you've got the gene, you're stuffed. We need guarantees before we hand over our blood, right?

Telemedicine is the big thing now. Doctor on a screen. But the broadband in Ceredigion is shocking. The video freezes just as you're showing them your rash. It creates a two-tier system: good health for those with fibre, bad health for those with copper wire. Tidy?

Welsh gov wants to track every single lamb with a digital tag. GPS and all sorts. Cost a fortune, it will. And for what? So some suit in Cardiff can watch dots on a screen? My dog knows where the sheep are. It's solving a problem that doesn't exist and bankrupting the small farms in the process.

Rewilding schemes, right? They've got algorithms deciding which land should be returned to nature for carbon credits. The computer says my top field is 'low yield', so it should be trees. But my family has worked that land for 300 years. An algorithm doesn't know the soil like I do. Is it right to farm by spreadsheet?

Bought a new tractor, John Deere. Lovely bit of kit. But it breaks down and I can't fix it with a spanner. Needs a laptop and a proprietary code. Have to wait a week for a technician from England. I'm losing the harvest waiting for a software update. We need the Right to Repair, don't we?

These carbon trading apps. Big companies buying up Welsh farms to plant trees and offset their pollution. The app makes it easy, click of a button. But it's hollow out the rural communities. No farmers, no school, no pub, just trees and sensors. Is that a green future or a dead one?

Drones for mustering the sheep. Saves the legs, aye. But the sheepdog is part of the family. If we replace the dogs with drones, we lose the training, the bond, the tradition. Some things are worth more than efficiency, surely?

Virtual fencing for the cattle. They wear collars that shock them if they cross a GPS line. No physical fences needed. But if the GPS goes down, the cows are on the A470. And is it cruel to zap a cow because the satellite drifted? I don't trust it, see.

They're gene-editing the Welsh Black cattle to be more methane efficient. Patented genes. If my bull mates with a neighbor's cow, do I owe a corporation royalties for the calf? It's turning nature into intellectual property.

Robotic shearing is coming. 'Safer for the sheep', they say. But shearing is a community event, everyone helps out, bit of food, bit of a laugh. If we automate it, the isolation up here gets even worse. We need neighbors, not just machines, isn't it?

Council's put smart cams all round Bute Street and the Docks, fam. They say it's for 'traffic management' by the Noor, but we all know it's facial rec scanning the uncles going to prayer. Do we smash the sensors or try to jam the signal with IR lights?

These new property developers in the Bay are using AI to map 'antisocial hotspots' to lower insurance premiums for the new flats. But they're flagging our community centre as a 'high risk zone' just cause the boys hang out outside. How do we fight an algo that thinks our culture is a crime risk?

Feds are using some predictive software in Grangetown now, see. It's targeting Somali lads for stop and search based on 'historical data' from when the area was rougher. It's a self-fulfilling prophecy, innit? The more they search, the more data they get.

Museum wants to digitise the oral histories of the Tiger Bay elders, which is lush, but they want to own the copyright and train their 'Cardiff accent' AI on it. That voice belongs to the community, not some tech startup in London.

Youth club in Butetown got funding, but the condition is installing biometric entry systems. Most of the Yemeni parents aren't having it—don't want their kids' fingerprints on a database shared with the Home Office. Do we take the money and the surveillance, or stay broke?

Housing association in the Bay is fitting 'smart meters' that track occupancy. They reckon it's for energy efficiency, but it feels like they're checking how many relatives we got staying over. It's spying on our hospitality, straight up.

Applied for a job in the city centre, mind. The AI video interview rejected me. My cousin reckons it's cause the software can't handle the Cardiff Somali accent—thinks we're aggressive when we're just talking normal. Is it worth appealing or is the system rigged?

There's a 'Safe Streets' app everyone in the Bay is using to report issues. Problem is, the new posh residents are flagging 'loitering' every time three black boys stand on a corner. The app auto-forwards to police. It's digital gentrification, turning neighbours into narcs.

Local Facebook group for the valley is absolutely buzzing with bots chopsing about 'gangs' every time a brown face walks past the welfare hall. Admin won't delete it, says it's 'free speech'. It's making my nan scared to leave the house. Do we hack the group or what?

Living up the top of the Rhondda, signal is shocking. Now the GP wants us to do video consults only. My mum's English isn't great, and the connection cuts out every ten seconds. She's not getting treated cause the tech doesn't work in the valleys. Is that not negligence?

Walking home from the train station in the dark, using this safety app. It keeps diverting me away from 'high crime' areas, which happens to be the only street where other Asians live. It's routing me through the pitch black woods instead. The algo is racist and it's gonna get me hurt.
