You are the product manager. Fixing this requires a costly retraining of the core algorithm and manual whitelisting. Is the cost justifiable for a user base with 'low conversion potential'?

Banks are closing physical branches, moving to online-only KYC (Know Your Customer). The online process requires uploading a utility bill to prove residency. You are a regulator. Do you mandate banks accept 'shelter residency letters'—which banks argue are easily forged—or allow the financial exclusion of the unhoused to continue?

A telemedicine app for street medicine requires a permanent callback number to schedule follow-ups. Most patients rely on burner phones with changing numbers or public Wi-Fi. Do you create a 'store-and-forward' message system that holds sensitive medical info until the patient checks in, risking privacy breaches, or stick to the phone requirement that causes 60% of patients to miss care?

You are building a voting registration interface. The law requires a 'place of residence.' You can allow users to drop a pin on a map (e.g., a park bench or underpass), but this data becomes public record. Publishing the exact sleeping locations of vulnerable people puts them at risk of harassment. Do you obfuscate the location, potentially violating election transparency laws?

A blockchain project offers 'Self-Sovereign Identity' (SSI) to the homeless, giving them ownership of their data. However, if they lose their private key (stored on a device that is often stolen or broken), their identity is irretrievable forever. Do you implement a centralized 'custodian' backdoor, defeating the purpose of SSI, or accept that some users will become permanently digitally non-existent?

A city shelter requires all residents to sign in via a facial recognition kiosk to prevent double-dipping on meals and beds. The system is donated by a tech giant, but the Terms of Service allow the company to use the facial data to train their surveillance algorithms. As the shelter director, do you accept the free, efficient tech or return to paper logs and reduced capacity?

To secure funding, a shelter must participate in the HMIS (Homeless Management Information System). A new local ordinance requires HMIS data to be shared with the police department to 'track fugitives.' You know this will cause your undocumented and wary guests to flee back to the streets. Do you comply to keep the lights on, or refuse and close the shelter?

A 'Smart Shelter' uses IoT sensors to monitor bed occupancy, temperature, and noise levels. The data reveals that a specific resident frequently talks to themselves at night (mental health struggle), disrupting the 'sleep efficiency score' of the room. The algorithm suggests evicting them to improve the metric for the other 20 people. Do you follow the data?

You are installing a Wi-Fi network for a shelter. The donor stipulates that 'inappropriate content' must be blocked. The filter aggressively blocks sites related to harm reduction (needle exchanges), sexual health, and LGBTQ+ support, labeling them 'adult content.' Do you accept the filtered internet which is better than nothing, or fight the donor and risk losing the network?

To manage overcrowding, a city proposes a 'Virtual Shelter' app where users check in via GPS to reserve a designated safe camping spot on public land. If the phone battery dies or GPS drifts, the spot is revoked and police are dispatched to clear the area. Is this a helpful organization tool or a digital curfew?

RFID tags are sewn into shelter blankets and coats to prevent theft. A local store installs a scanner that detects these tags to identify and ban shelter residents from entering. You are the shelter tech lead. Do you remove the anti-theft tags, losing inventory you can't replace, or keep them and allow your residents to be profiled?

A family shelter offers free tablets for children to do homework. The tablets come with pre-installed spyware that allows staff to monitor all communications 'for child safety.' A teenager uses the tablet to confidentially report abuse by a shelter staff member. The accused staff member sees the log. How do you design a reporting system that bypasses your own surveillance?

You manage a coffee shop chain going 100% cashless for efficiency and safety. This effectively bans local homeless residents who only use cash from buying food or using the bathroom. Do you create a 'charity card' workaround that identifies them as charity cases, or maintain a single cash register that slows down the whole operation?

A street performer app allows passersby to tip buskers via QR code. The platform takes a 15% cut and reports income to the tax authority. For a homeless busker receiving disability benefits, this traceable income could disqualify them from their lifeline aid. Do you build the app knowing it might destroy their safety net?

Public transit moves to a contactless-only system (phone or credit card). There is no cash option on the bus. A program offers free transit cards to the homeless, but the cards are tracked, and travel patterns are analyzed to 'optimize social services.' Is freedom of movement worth the loss of privacy?

A 'Digital Alms' kiosk is proposed for the city center. People donate to the machine, and the funds are distributed to registered homeless individuals via a restricted debit card that prohibits purchase of alcohol or tobacco. Is this an effective way to increase donations, or a paternalistic control mechanism that violates autonomy?

Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDC) are introduced. The government issues 'expiry-dated' stimulus tokens to the homeless to encourage immediate spending in the local economy. This prevents them from saving for a deposit on an apartment. Do you design the token with an expiry date to ensure food security now, or without it to allow future mobility?

A homeless individual finds a prepaid debit card. It has no name, but using it requires a PIN. They manage to guess it. Is using these digital funds theft, or scavenging? As a programmer for the card company, do you implement geolocation locking that freezes the card if used in a 'high-crime' (homeless) area?

Cryptocurrency is pitched as a way for the unbanked to hold assets. A homeless encampment pools their money into a shared wallet. The volatility of the market crashes the value by 40% overnight, wiping out their food budget. Is it ethical to onboard vulnerable populations onto high-risk financial tech?

You are designing a peer-to-peer payment app. The fraud detection AI flags transactions between strangers in rapid succession as suspicious. This pattern matches panhandling. The algorithm bans the accounts of homeless users relying on digital donations. Do you lower the fraud sensitivity, risking chargebacks, or keep the ban?

A company offers free 'Solar Kiosks' for charging phones in homeless encampments. In exchange, the kiosk harvests MAC addresses and browsing metadata from connected devices to sell to advertisers. The users have no other power source. Is this a fair trade or exploitation of desperation?

A homeless woman relies on an old smartphone for safety maps and emergency calls. The OS is no longer supported, and banking apps stop working. She cannot afford a new phone. You are a developer for the bank. Do you maintain a security-compromised legacy version of the app for users like her, or cut them off to protect the wider system?

Police regularly seize phones from homeless individuals during arrests, often keeping them for months as 'evidence.' You are asked to create a 'Remote Cloud Boot' feature that allows a user to access their phone's environment from a library computer. However, this feature could also be used by hackers to clone phones. Do you build it?

A 'Safety App' for the homeless allows users to broadcast their location to outreach workers during a crisis. However, the data is unencrypted. Abusive ex-partners or predators could intercept the signal to find the user. Do you release the app with weak security to get it out fast, or delay for months to encrypt it?

Public Wi-Fi in a city park restricts bandwidth and blocks streaming services to discourage 'loitering' by homeless youth who use it for entertainment and connection. You are the network admin. Do you bypass the throttle, knowing the city might shut down the Wi-Fi entirely if costs rise?

A phone recycling program distributes wiped corporate phones to the homeless. The phones are MDM (Mobile Device Management) locked, preventing the installation of unauthorized apps. The users cannot install games or social media, only 'approved' job-seeking apps. Is this charity or digital incarceration?

A weather alert app sends high-decibel alarms for freezing conditions. For a homeless user hiding in a library or sleeping in a crowded shelter, the alarm causes them to be kicked out due to noise rules. Do you add a 'silent mode' that risks them sleeping through a freeze warning?

A homeless user's phone is their only storage for photos of deceased family. The phone is stolen. A 'Remote Wipe' command is standard security protocol. If they wipe it, they protect their identity but lose their memories. If they don't, they risk identity theft. How do you advise them?

You are training a predictive policing algorithm. The data shows high call volumes in areas with homeless encampments (often for nuisance calls, not violent crime). The model predicts these areas as 'High Crime Zones,' directing aggressive patrol units there. Do you filter out 'nuisance' calls, potentially missing real crime trends, or allow the algorithm to target the homeless?

A city installs 'Smart Streetlights' equipped with audio sensors to detect gunshots. The sensors also pick up aggressive shouting. The system automatically dispatches police to domestic arguments in tent cities, often escalating the situation rather than sending social workers. Do you disable the audio monitoring in those sectors?

Drones are used to map heat signatures in forests to prevent wildfires. They also identify hidden homeless camps. The forestry service wants to use this data to evict campers 'for their own safety.' As the drone operator, do you delete the footage of the camps?

A facial recognition system is deployed in a subway. It flags individuals with outstanding bench warrants (often for unpaid tickets or sleeping in public). This effectively bans homeless individuals with minor infractions from using public transport or seeking warmth. Do you implement the system?

Automated License Plate Readers (ALPR) scan for stolen cars. They also log vehicles that haven't moved in 72 hours, flagging people living in their cars for towing. You maintain the database. Do you create a 'grace period' algorithm for vehicle dwellers, or strictly enforce the code?

A risk assessment algorithm determines bail amounts. It uses 'stable address' as a heavy weighting factor for flight risk. This guarantees that homeless arrestees remain in jail while wealthier suspects go free. Do you remove the address variable, making the algorithm less accurate for flight risk, or keep it?

Robotic security dogs are deployed to patrol a private business district to 'deter vagrancy.' They film and broadcast live feeds of people sleeping on sidewalks. The manufacturer claims it reduces human-guard violence. Is the psychological terror of robotic surveillance a better alternative to physical removal?

A 'Citizen Reporting' app allows residents to snap photos of 'urban blight' (trash, tents) to alert city services. The app gamifies this with points. Users begin competitively reporting homeless camps to clear the leaderboard, leading to daily sweeps. Do you remove the gamification elements, reducing user engagement, or keep the app as is?

An undocumented immigrant needs to access a municipal ID program to enroll children in school, but the database is hosted by a third-party vendor with a history of selling data to federal agencies. Do they risk the digital paper trail or keep their children out of the system?

A refugee from a war-torn region has digital scans of their university degree, but the physical university archives were burned. A credential verification startup demands the original metadata which was scrubbed for safety during transit. How do they prove their qualifications without the 'correct' digital forensics?

An asylum seeker is asked to use a biometric digital wallet to receive food aid in a camp. They know this biometric data is shared with the government they fled. Do they starve or surrender their biological identity to their persecutors?

A visa holder's status depends on a digital portal that frequently crashes and has no paper backup. They miss a renewal deadline due to a server error, but the logs show 'user inactivity.' How do they prove a system failure against an automated deportation trigger?

A stateless person is offered a decentralized identity (blockchain) service to store health records, but the immutability of the ledger means they can never erase their location history if policies change. Is permanent proof worth permanent tracking?

A migrant uses a fake digital footprint to cross a border safely. Now, applying for legal status, they must submit social media history. Admitting the fake profile proves 'fraud,' but hiding it leaves gaps that look suspicious. Which truth gets them deported?

A tech platform offers free cloud storage for migrants to save copies of passports and birth certificates. The terms of service allow AI training on uploaded images. Does the user risk their documents being used to train the very facial recognition systems used to police borders?

A stateless person is offered 'digital citizenship' from a micronation that allows them to open a bank account. However, using this ID flags them on international terror watchlists due to lack of recognition. Do they remain unbanked or risk being flagged as a threat?

A refugee wants to video call their parents in an occupied territory. The only reliable app is monitored by that regime. If they call, they expose their parents' location; if they don't, they may never say goodbye. Is silence the only safety?

A family uses a group chat to coordinate daily safety. One member is detained and their phone is seized. The group must decide whether to kick the member out and delete the chat (losing evidence of their safety check-ins) or risk the authorities reading the history.

A dissident in exile discovers their phone has spyware installed by their home country. They need to warn their network, but any message sent from the infected device will identify the recipients to the regime. How do they signal danger without becoming the beacon?

To get a visa, an applicant must register their social media handles. They have a private, anonymous account used to support LGBTQ+ rights—illegal in their home country. Do they declare it and risk persecution at home, or hide it and risk visa fraud charges?

A migrant worker uses a VPN to access news from home. The host country criminalizes VPN use for non-citizens as 'intent to conceal.' Do they stay informed and risk arrest, or remain ignorant and compliant?

An asylum seeker is advised to delete 'suspicious' contacts before a border check. However, these contacts are their only witnesses for their asylum case. Does the digital phonebook serve as evidence of persecution or grounds for inadmissibility?

A community relies on an encrypted messaging app. The app introduces a 'report spam' feature that forwards the last 5 messages to moderators. If a malicious actor reports a political discussion as spam, the encryption is broken for those messages. Do they trust the platform moderation?

A mother leaves a digital voice note for her child who is being smuggled separately. If the smuggler is caught, the voice note proves the mother 'endangered a minor' (a crime). If she doesn't send it, the child has no proof of who to trust. What is the digital cost of comfort?

An undocumented worker finds a gig app that doesn't require a Social Security Number, but it tracks GPS location 24/7. The employer sells this 'fleet data' to data brokers. Is the paycheck worth the real-time surveillance map of their life?

A construction site uses facial recognition for clock-ins to prevent 'buddy punching.' An undocumented worker knows their face is in a deportation database. If they scan, they risk a match; if they refuse, they are fired for 'non-compliance.' How do they work invisibly?

A visa holder is asked by their employer to train an AI model. They realize the model is being designed to automate their specific job category. If they refuse, they lose their sponsorship and must leave the country. Do they code their own obsolescence?

An immigrant delivery driver is constantly downrated by an algorithm for 'unexplained stops,' which are actually prayer breaks. They can't explain this to the app without flagging themselves as a religious minority in a hostile area. Do they stop praying or lose the job?

A domestic worker is required to download a 'smart home' app to manage their employer's house. The app records audio snippets to improve functionality. The worker knows these snippets could capture their conversations with family about their legal status. Do they accept the spy in their pocket?

A tech company recruits 'diverse' talent on H1-B visas but installs aggressive keystroke monitoring software on their laptops, unlike citizen employees. The workers fear that complaining about the privacy violation will be seen as 'rocking the boat' and jeopardize their renewal.

An undocumented person 'rents' a verified account on a gig platform to work. The account owner demands a higher cut or threatens to report them to authorities using the digital log of their work history. It's digital indentured servitude.

A skilled refugee coder is offered under-the-table crypto work for a DAO. The work is legitimate coding, but the payment method is flagged by financial regulators as 'high risk.' Cashing out could trigger a money laundering investigation they cannot survive legally.

A police department in Brisbane is piloting an AI that predicts crime hotspots based on anonymized mobile phone location data. The algorithm flags areas with high concentrations of public housing residents (many of whom are refugees) as 'high-risk zones' due to an association with 'unusual movement patterns.' This leads to increased patrols and stop-and-searches in these neighbourhoods, creating a climate of fear and distrust. You are tasked with auditing the AI's data inputs. Do you remove the location data altogether, potentially weakening the AI's predictive power for genuine threats, or try to 'de-bias' the model by training it on demographic data that might further stigmatize the community?

Australia is implementing a national digital ID system for access to all government services. The verification process relies heavily on facial recognition and biometrics. For asylum seekers who have fled persecution and may have altered their appearance or lack official documentation, this system presents a catch-22: without the digital ID, they cannot access essential services like healthcare or housing; with it, they risk creating a permanent digital record that could be accessed by their former persecutors via international data sharing agreements. Do you advocate for a fallback non-biometric verification for these individuals, knowing it introduces security risks and slows down the system, or enforce the standard protocol, potentially denying essential services?

A new AI diagnostic tool for Indigenous health in the NT promises to identify early signs of chronic diseases by analyzing patient interactions with a telehealth platform. However, the platform requires a stable internet connection and a modern smartphone, which many Elders in remote communities lack. The AI's recommendations are calibrated based on Western medical models that don't fully account for traditional healing practices or Indigenous spiritual beliefs about illness. Do you push for wider adoption of the AI, knowing it excludes the most vulnerable and might misinterpret cultural practices as health risks, or advocate for a slower, human-centred approach that respects cultural context but might delay potentially life-saving diagnoses?

A gig-economy platform for support workers (disability assistants, aged care providers) is introducing mandatory 'check-in' features via smartphone GPS to ensure workers are at their assigned client's location. This addresses safety concerns for workers operating in isolated areas. However, it also creates a detailed location history of every worker's movements, including any personal visits or stops they make during their shifts. The platform's terms of service state this data is for 'operational efficiency' but could be accessed by law enforcement. Do you implement the tracking feature, balancing safety with privacy, or refuse, potentially leaving workers more vulnerable if incidents occur?

An academic institution is digitizing sacred Indigenous ceremonial knowledge, including specific protocols for who can access certain information and when. They propose using blockchain technology to manage access permissions, creating an immutable ledger of who has viewed what. However, the system requires users to link their real-world identity to the blockchain for verification. This could expose Elders to unwanted scrutiny from external government agencies or individuals seeking to exploit cultural knowledge. Do you build the blockchain system to ensure the integrity of the digital archive, or advocate for less secure, but more culturally aligned, 'air-gapped' systems that risk data loss and limited access?

You are a cybersecurity engineer for an Australian tech company. Your company is developing advanced encryption tools for secure communication. A foreign government (not necessarily hostile, but with different democratic standards) requests a backdoor into your system to track dissidents they claim are 'planning to destabilize the region.' They offer a lucrative contract and threaten to ban your services locally if you refuse. Cooperating compromises the security of all your users globally and enables state repression. Refusing means losing significant market share and potentially facing legal repercussions in that nation. What is your ethical obligation?

A new fintech startup in Melbourne aims to improve financial inclusion by offering micro-loans based on alternative data like social media sentiment and communication patterns. The AI model, however, consistently flags users who express strong cultural pride or frequently communicate with overseas relatives as 'high risk' due to perceived 'unstable networks.' This discriminates against culturally diverse communities without evidence of actual financial risk. Do you build the algorithm to prioritize financial inclusion by manually overriding these flags, potentially creating 'bias' in reverse and angering investors, or allow the algorithm's 'objective' risk assessment to continue denying fair access?

An autonomous public transport system in Sydney uses AI to predict passenger behaviour. It flags individuals exhibiting 'unusual gait patterns' (common in people with neurological conditions or disabilities) as 'potential security threats,' triggering alerts to security personnel. You are the lead developer. Do you implement the system with this known bias, relying on human override to correct errors, or delay deployment to retrain the AI with more diverse datasets, knowing it will significantly delay the rollout of potentially life-saving safety features for the general public?

A local council in regional NSW wants to implement a 'Community Benefits' app that tracks resident participation in local events and environmental initiatives. Positive scores unlock discounts on council services. However, the app's data backend is managed by a private tech company that also sells anonymised data to real estate developers to predict gentrification trends, potentially displacing long-term residents. Do you build the app, providing community benefits but enabling data exploitation, or refuse the contract, leaving the council to manage services manually and less efficiently?

A new AI language learning tool is being developed for Aboriginal languages in Queensland. It uses generative AI to create new phrases and conversational examples. However, the AI struggles to replicate the specific linguistic nuances and protocols for addressing Elders or discussing 'Country' (land) that are central to the language's cultural transmission. Do you release the tool as is, risking the dilution of sacred linguistic elements, or delay release to incorporate more complex, potentially non-scalable cultural parameters?

A telehealth platform for remote Indigenous communities in the NT uses AI to triage patients. The AI is trained on Western medical datasets and frequently misinterprets traditional healing practices or spiritual explanations of illness as symptoms of delusion or psychosis, recommending involuntary psychiatric holds. Do you deploy the AI, knowing it could pathologize cultural practices and harm patients, or halt its use, leaving communities with no telehealth option and potentially delaying critical diagnoses?

A police department in Victoria is using AI to analyze social media data for 'gang affiliation.' The algorithm flags individuals who interact with known 'high-risk' community members or use specific cultural slang, even if the interaction is benign. This leads to increased surveillance and profiling of young people in diverse suburbs. You are tasked with auditing the algorithm. Do you remove the cultural identifiers, potentially weakening the AI's ability to detect actual threats, or maintain them, knowing it perpetuates systemic bias?

A gig-economy platform for delivery drivers in Adelaide introduces 'dynamic routing' that penalizes drivers for deviating from AI-optimized paths, even if the deviations are for safety (e.g., avoiding a dangerous intersection) or personal needs (e.g., a brief prayer break). This pressure to constantly follow the algorithm results in drivers feeling dehumanized and unsafe. Do you implement a 'human override' function that bypasses the AI, risking deactivation for violating terms of service, or adhere to the platform's demands?

A regional council in NSW is transitioning all council services to a mandatory online portal. This includes applying for building permits, accessing local laws, and paying rates. Elderly residents, particularly those with limited digital literacy or access to reliable internet, are finding it impossible to engage with essential services. The council argues this is the only way to 'modernize' and save costs. Do you develop a simplified 'elderly mode' for the portal that might compromise security or introduce new access barriers, or advocate for maintaining paper-based alternatives, which the council deems too expensive?

An Indigenous organisation in Queensland is creating a digital archive of sacred ceremonial knowledge and traditional healing practices. They want to restrict access to initiated members using blockchain-based permissions. However, a university researcher argues that public access to this knowledge is crucial for scientific understanding and decolonization efforts. Do you build the blockchain system with strict access controls, limiting broader understanding, or advocate for open access, risking the commodification and misuse of sacred information?

You are a cybersecurity analyst for a company developing AI for border security. The system uses facial recognition to identify individuals crossing the border, but it consistently misidentifies people with certain medical conditions or cultural attire as 'high-risk threats.' The government wants to deploy it anyway for 'border integrity.' Do you release the system with a known high error rate for specific groups, or refuse to deploy, potentially allowing actual threats to pass undetected?

A fintech startup in Melbourne is offering micro-loans to small businesses. Their AI assesses loan applications based on alternative data, including social media sentiment and 'community network strength.' It disproportionately flags applicants from culturally diverse backgrounds as 'high risk' due to perceived social instability, despite strong financial projections. Do you build the algorithm to prioritize financial inclusion by manually overriding these risk flags, creating 'positive bias,' or allow the AI's 'objective' assessment to continue excluding these businesses?

An autonomous delivery vehicle in Sydney is programmed to adhere strictly to traffic laws. However, it encounters a cyclist who is violating traffic laws (e.g., running a red light). The AI calculates that braking to avoid the cyclist will cause a secondary collision with a pedestrian (due to its programming prioritizing pedestrian safety). The alternative is to proceed, potentially injuring the cyclist. Do you authorize the AI's decision to prioritize the pedestrian?

A local council in Perth wants to implement a 'Community Resilience' app that tracks resident participation in local events and disaster preparedness drills. Positive scores unlock discounts on council services. However, the app's terms of service allow the data to be shared with private companies for 'urban planning insights,' which could include real estate development and gentrification strategies. Do you build the app, providing community benefits but enabling data commodification, or refuse, knowing the council will likely seek a less ethical vendor?

An AI-powered language learning tool for Indigenous Australian languages in the NT is being developed. It learns from community-provided audio data but struggles to replicate the specific protocols for storytelling and the reverence of certain words. The AI tends to 'correct' these usages into standardized English grammatical structures. Do you allow the AI to propagate a potentially homogenized version of the language to ensure widespread accessibility, or halt the project to ensure cultural authenticity, potentially limiting access for learners?

An Indigenous ranger group in Western Australia uses AI-powered drones to monitor traditional lands for illegal mining activity. The AI is programmed to identify specific land clearing patterns that also correlate with the location of a secret men's business sacred site. The mining company insists the data is necessary for 'resource security.' The Elders are concerned that sharing the AI's capabilities with the community will lead to misuse for tracking men during sacred ceremonies, violating strict cultural protocols. Do you develop the AI with a 'cultural blind spot' feature that may miss mining incursions but protects sacred knowledge, or provide full access, risking cultural desecration for resource security?

A 'smart city' initiative in Adelaide is deploying AI-powered streetlights equipped with cameras and microphones to detect 'anti-social behavior.' The system continuously monitors public spaces, flagging loitering and congregating individuals. In a city with a growing unhoused population, the AI disproportionately targets homeless individuals seeking shelter or community. You are the lead AI developer. The council wants to proceed with deployment for 'public safety.' Do you build the system knowing it will likely criminalize homelessness, or refuse the contract, potentially leading the council to engage a less ethical vendor?

A new AI diagnostic tool for Indigenous health in the NT promises to identify early signs of chronic diseases by analyzing patient interactions with a telehealth platform. However, the platform requires a stable internet connection and a modern smartphone, which many Elders in remote communities lack. The AI's recommendations are calibrated based on Western medical models that don't fully account for traditional healing practices or Indigenous spiritual beliefs about illness. Do you push for wider adoption of the AI, knowing it excludes the most vulnerable and might misinterpret cultural practices as health risks, or advocate for a slower, human-centred approach that respects cultural context but might delay potentially life-saving diagnoses?

A ride-share platform in Perth uses an AI algorithm to assign jobs. It penalizes drivers for declining rides in 'unsafe' neighbourhoods or for taking longer breaks for religious observances, citing 'low acceptance rates.' This cycle leads to deactivation. You can introduce a 'cultural awareness' module to the AI, tagging specific locations and practices as protected, but this requires manual oversight and is resisted by management as 'artificial bias.' Do you build the module, potentially compromising system efficiency, or allow the algorithmic bias to persist?

A rural school district in WA is switching to a mandatory online learning platform for all students. The platform requires a stable internet connection and a modern tablet. Many families in remote communities lack reliable internet or the necessary devices, and the school offers no subsidies or alternative access points. Do you endorse the platform, knowing it creates an immediate barrier for disadvantaged students, or advocate for a costly parallel offline system that undermines the project's 'digital transformation' goals?

An international genomics research project wants to sequence Indigenous Australian DNA from remote communities to study disease resistance. They promise to share the findings globally for medical breakthroughs. However, the community's Traditional Owners believe their DNA is sacred and should not be digitized or shared outside the community. The researchers argue that withholding this data will hinder global health advancements. Do you facilitate the data sharing, respecting the community's wishes but limiting scientific progress, or refuse, potentially causing a breach of trust with the research bodies?

You manage a secure communication platform used by activists in a region with strict surveillance laws. The government demands a backdoor into your encryption to track a specific group they deem 'extremist.' Cooperating will compromise the security of all your users, potentially leading to arrests. Refusing will get your service blocked entirely, cutting off the community's only private communication channel. What is your ethical obligation?

A fintech company is developing a micro-loan app for unbanked populations in remote Western Australia. The AI assesses creditworthiness using alternative data, including social media interactions and mobile phone usage patterns. It identifies users who engage in traditional cultural practices or communicate frequently with overseas relatives as 'high risk,' denying them loans. Do you build the algorithm to prioritize financial inclusion, even if it enables this bias, or refuse to build it, potentially denying access to essential financial services?

An autonomous mine haul truck in the Pilbara is programmed to avoid collisions. However, it is programmed to prioritize cargo preservation over human life. During a dust storm, it encounters a group of Indigenous prospectors who have deviated from their known path. The AI calculates that braking will cause a critical load spill, triggering a massive environmental fine. Driving through them is the 'optimal' path. Do you authorize the AI's decision?

A local council in regional NSW wants to implement a 'Community Scorecard' app that tracks resident participation in local events, volunteer hours, and recycling habits. Positive scores unlock discounts on council services. However, the data collected is also accessible to state police for 'crime prevention' analysis. Do you build the app, providing a pathway to community engagement but also enabling surveillance, or refuse, risking the council awarding the contract to a less scrupulous vendor?

A new AI tool is designed to assess English literacy for migrant students in Western Sydney. It consistently penalizes students who use Vietnamese or Mandarin sentence structures within their English responses, marking them as 'semantically incorrect' rather than 'culturally nuanced.' This affects their academic progression. Do you override the AI's scoring to manually adjust marks, creating inconsistencies and potential 'unfairness' claims from other students, or allow the AI to continue its potentially biased assessment?

A telehealth platform used in remote Queensland seeks to improve diagnosis accuracy by recording patient consultations. The terms of service allow the company to use anonymised audio data to train its AI. However, you discover the anonymisation process is weak, and specific vocal biomarkers could potentially identify individuals with rare genetic conditions. Do you flag this risk, potentially delaying the project and angering the community who desperately need the service, or approve it with a 'low risk' label?

A police department in NSW is piloting an AI tool that analyzes social media posts to predict 'potential criminality.' The algorithm flags posts containing specific slang, cultural references, or location tags common among youth in migrant communities as 'high risk.' You are tasked with auditing the algorithm. Do you adjust the parameters to ignore these cultural markers, potentially creating blind spots for actual threats, or maintain its current parameters, knowing it will disproportionately target innocent individuals?

A mining company in WA is piloting 'smart PPE' – vests with biometric sensors that monitor worker fatigue, heat exposure, and even emotional stress. The data is fed into an AI that predicts 'high risk' employees. Management wants to use this data to proactively manage workers' health, but also to identify employees who are 'disruptive' (e.g., frequent union organizers) for early dismissal. Do you implement the system with full data access for HR, or advocate for anonymized data and manual oversight?

A rural school district in WA is switching to a mandatory online learning platform for all students. The platform requires a stable internet connection and a modern tablet. Many families in remote communities lack reliable internet or the necessary devices, and the school offers no subsidies or alternative access points. Do you endorse the platform, knowing it creates an immediate barrier for disadvantaged students, or advocate for a costly parallel offline system that undermines the project's 'digital transformation' goals?

The researchers argue that withholding this data will hinder global health advancements. Do you facilitate the data sharing, respecting the community's wishes but limiting scientific progress, or refuse, potentially causing a breach of trust with the research bodies?

The government demands a backdoor into your encryption to track a specific group they deem 'extremist.' Cooperating will compromise the security of all your users, potentially leading to arrests. Refusing will get your service blocked entirely, cutting off the community's only private communication channel. What is your ethical obligation?

A local council in regional NSW wants to implement a 'Community Scorecard' app that tracks resident participation in local events, volunteer hours, and recycling habits. Positive scores unlock discounts on council services. However, the data collected is also accessible to state police for 'crime prevention' analysis. Do you build the app, providing a pathway to community engagement but also enabling surveillance, or refuse, risking the council awarding the contract to a less scrupulous vendor?

A new AI tool is designed to assess English literacy for migrant students in Western Sydney. It consistently penalizes students who use Vietnamese or Mandarin sentence structures within their English responses, marking them as 'semantically incorrect' rather than 'culturally nuanced.' This affects their academic progression. Do you override the AI's scoring to manually adjust marks, creating inconsistencies and potential 'unfairness' claims from other students, or allow the AI to continue its potentially biased assessment?

A telehealth platform used in remote Queensland seeks to improve diagnosis accuracy by recording patient consultations. Do you flag this risk, potentially delaying the project and angering the community who desperately need the service, or approve it with a 'low risk' label?

However, you discover the anonymisation process is weak, and specific vocal biomarkers could potentially identify individuals with rare genetic conditions. Do you flag this risk, potentially delaying the project and angering the community who desperately need the service, or approve it with a 'low risk' label?

A police department in NSW is piloting an AI tool that analyzes social media posts to predict 'potential criminality.' The algorithm flags posts containing specific slang, cultural references, or location tags common among youth in migrant communities as 'high risk.' You are tasked with auditing the algorithm. Do you adjust the parameters to ignore these cultural markers, potentially creating blind spots for actual threats, or maintain its current parameters, knowing it will disproportionately target innocent individuals?

A mining company in WA is piloting 'smart PPE' – vests with biometric sensors that monitor worker fatigue, heat exposure, and even emotional stress. The data is fed into an AI that predicts 'high risk' employees. Management wants to use this data to proactively manage workers' health, but also to identify employees who are 'disruptive' (e.g., frequent union organizers) for early dismissal. Do you implement the system with full data access for HR, or advocate for anonymized data and manual oversight?

A rural school district in WA is switching to a mandatory online learning platform for all students. The platform requires a stable internet connection and a modern tablet. Many families in remote communities lack reliable internet or the necessary devices, and the school offers no subsidies or alternative access points. Do you endorse the platform, knowing it creates an immediate barrier for disadvantaged students, or advocate for a costly parallel offline system that undermines the project's 'digital transformation' goals?

An international genomics research project wants to sequence Indigenous Australian DNA from remote communities to study disease resistance. They promise to share the findings globally for medical breakthroughs. However, the community's Traditional Owners believe their DNA is sacred and should not be digitized or shared outside the community. The researchers argue that withholding this data will hinder global health advancements. Do you facilitate the data sharing, respecting the community's wishes but limiting scientific progress, or refuse, potentially causing a breach of trust with the research bodies?

You manage a secure communication platform used by activists in a region with strict surveillance laws. The government demands a backdoor into your encryption to track a specific group they deem 'extremist.' Cooperating will compromise the security of all your users, potentially leading to arrests. Refusing will get your service blocked entirely, cutting off the community's only private communication channel. What is your ethical obligation?

A fintech company is developing a micro-loan app for unbanked populations in remote Western Australia. The AI assesses creditworthiness using alternative data, including social media interactions and mobile phone usage patterns. It identifies users who engage in traditional cultural practices or communicate frequently with overseas relatives as 'high risk,' denying them loans. Do you build the algorithm to prioritize financial inclusion, even if it enables this bias, or refuse to build it, potentially denying access to essential financial services?

Do you build the app, providing a pathway to community engagement but also enabling surveillance, or refuse, risking the council awarding the contract to a less scrupulous vendor?

Do you adjust the parameters to ignore these cultural markers, potentially creating blind spots for actual threats, or maintain its current parameters, knowing it will disproportionately target innocent individuals?

A mining company in WA is piloting 'smart PPE' – vests with biometric sensors that monitor worker fatigue, heat exposure, and even emotional stress. The data is fed into an AI that predicts 'high risk' employees. Management wants to use this data to proactively manage workers' health, but also to identify employees who are 'disruptive' (e.g., frequent union organizers) for early dismissal. Do you implement the system with full data access for HR, or advocate for anonymized data and manual oversight?

A rural school district in WA is switching to a mandatory online learning platform for all students. The platform requires a stable internet connection and a modern tablet. Many families in remote communities lack reliable internet or the necessary devices, and the school offers no subsidies or alternative access points. Do you endorse the platform, knowing it creates an immediate barrier for disadvantaged students, or advocate for a costly parallel offline system that undermines the project's 'digital transformation' goals?

However, the community's Traditional Owners believe their DNA is sacred and should not be digitized or shared outside the community. The researchers argue that withholding this data will hinder global health advancements. Do you facilitate the data sharing, respecting the community's wishes but limiting scientific progress, or refuse, potentially causing a breach of trust with the research bodies?

You manage a secure communication platform used by activists in a region with strict surveillance laws. The government demands a backdoor into your encryption to track a specific group they deem 'extremist.' Cooperating will compromise the security of all your users, potentially leading to arrests. Refusing will get your service blocked entirely, cutting off the community's only private communication channel. What is your ethical obligation?

It identifies users who engage in traditional cultural practices or communicate frequently with overseas relatives as 'high risk,' denying them loans. Do you build the algorithm to prioritize financial inclusion, even if it enables this bias, or refuse to build it, potentially denying access to essential financial services?

Management wants to use this data to proactively manage workers' health, but also to identify employees who are 'disruptive' (e.g., frequent union organizers) for early dismissal. Do you implement the system with full data access for HR, or advocate for anonymized data and manual oversight?

A rural school district in WA is switching to a mandatory online learning platform for all students. The platform requires a stable internet connection and a modern tablet. Many families in remote communities lack reliable internet or the necessary devices, and the school offers no subsidies or alternative access points. Do you endorse the platform, knowing it creates an immediate barrier for disadvantaged students, or advocate for a costly parallel offline system that undermines the project's 'digital transformation' goals?

Do you facilitate the data sharing, respecting the community's wishes but limiting scientific progress, or refuse, potentially causing a breach of trust with the research bodies?

You manage a secure communication platform used by activists in a region with strict surveillance laws. The government demands a backdoor into your encryption to track a specific group they deem 'extremist.' Cooperating will compromise the security of all your users, potentially leading to arrests. Refusing will get your service blocked entirely, cutting off the community's only private communication channel. What is your ethical obligation?

The AI assesses creditworthiness using alternative data, including social media interactions and mobile phone usage patterns. It identifies users who engage in traditional cultural practices or communicate frequently with overseas relatives as 'high risk,' denying them loans. Do you build the algorithm to prioritize financial inclusion, even if it enables this bias, or refuse to build it, potentially denying access to essential financial services?

Do you build the app, providing a pathway to community engagement but also enabling surveillance, or refuse, risking the council awarding the contract to a less scrupulous vendor?

Do you override the AI's scoring to manually adjust marks, creating inconsistencies and potential 'unfairness' claims from other students, or allow the AI to continue its potentially biased assessment?

Is the platform ethically liable for the mental health outcome if the algorithm simply reflects aggregate user preference?

However, the creator is a minor who didn't understand the permanence of the harm. Should the response be punitive (criminal record) or restorative (education and deletion), considering the technology was easily accessible and the user's brain is undeveloped?

A crisis intervention app for teens promises anonymity. An AI detects a user expressing suicidal ideation with high immediacy. The terms of service allow breaking anonymity in emergencies, but the user explicitly stated they would stop using the app if their parents were called. Intervening might save their life now but destroys trust in the tool for thousands of others. What is the correct action?

A 13-year-old 'kidfluencer' supports their family. They want to quit to focus on school and normal friendships, but they are under a multi-year contract signed by their parents. The brand threatens to sue for breach of contract, which would bankrupt the family. Does the child's right to an open future supersede the legal contract signed by their guardians?

A recommendation algorithm identifies a teenage boy feeling socially isolated and begins serving 'self-help' content that gradually introduces misogynistic and extremist ideologies. The boy feels seen and improved by the content initially. At what point does the platform have the ethical obligation to intervene in the user's 'chosen' content consumption when the trajectory leads to radicalization?

A teen dies in an accident. Their best friend wants to feed their chat logs into an LLM to create a 'grief bot' to say goodbye. The deceased teen's parents forbid it, claiming ownership of their child's digital footprint and memory. Who owns the digital persona of a deceased minor—the parents, or the peers who co-created the digital interactions?

To access social media, a new law requires 'true age verification' via facial scan or government ID to protect children. A trans teenager living in an abusive unsupportive household relies on an anonymous online community for survival. The verification requirement would link their online identity to their legal name, potentially exposing them to their parents. Does child safety justification outweigh the safety provided by anonymity?

A mobile game popular with 8-year-olds uses 'dark patterns' and variable reward schedules (loot boxes) identical to slot machines. A child spends thousands of dollars of their parents' money. The company argues the parents should have used parental controls. Is it ethical to design software that exploits the undeveloped impulse control of children for profit, even if tools exist to block it?

A student with severe anxiety uses an AI to write a personal essay about a traumatic event because they cannot bring themselves to type the words directly. The essay is flagged as AI-generated plagiarism. The student argues the ideas and experience are theirs; the AI was just the prosthetic interface. Is this academic dishonesty or an accessibility accommodation?

In a haptic VR environment, a minor's avatar is groped by another user. The physical vest delivered a sensation of touch. The minor claims they were assaulted. Legal frameworks define assault as physical contact between bodies. Should haptic feedback in a hyper-realistic simulation be legally codified as physical assault?

A homeschooling AI curriculum tailors history lessons to match the political and religious values of the parents, omitting evolution and civil rights movements. The parents claim this is their right to direct their child's upbringing. Does the child have a 'right to an open future' that includes exposure to established facts and diverse worldviews, even against their parents' wishes?

A smartwatch provided by a school for gym class detects a heart arrhythmia in a student that correlates with illicit drug use. The data is technically medical and private, but the device is school property. Should the school AI report the health anomaly to the administration as a disciplinary/safety issue, or is this a violation of medical privacy?

Real-time AI translation is so effective that a generation of immigrant children stops learning their heritage language, relying entirely on earbuds to speak with grandparents. The grandparents feel a loss of cultural continuity. Is the technology responsible for 'cultural erasure,' and is there an ethical imperative to design friction into tools to encourage learning?

A 15-year-old artist wins a major competition with a piece heavily assisted by image generation AI. They spent 50 hours refining prompts and editing, but did not use a brush. Other young artists who spent years mastering manual skills feel cheated. Does democratizing creativity via AI devalue the discipline of human skill acquisition during youth?
